Week-by-week if you have a job

Assume evenings. This is two weeks to a used skill, not a prompt brand.

Week 1, days 1-2: write and test

One job you already run. Write the instructions. Run a real example. Run a broken example. Save both. You can do this in two evenings after work. Do not design a landing page yet. Do not name it after yourself.

Week 1, day 3: package and checkout

README, skill file, sample in, sample out. Zip. $19 Payment Link or Stan. Buy it from a second email. Record the 20-second screen on your phone if you have to. Filename after the job. Version v1.0 on the README.

Week 1, days 4-7: five asks, one post a day

Five personal messages. Post the screen recording once a day in one place — same clip, same offer. Help in two threads where people complain about the job. Link stays in the profile. Ask anyone who bought: did the sample run? Fix the install trip-up the same night.

Week 2: patch, then wait

Fix whatever the first buyer could not install. Ship v1.1. Email people who bought. Do not add a second skill until this one has a stranger sale. If nobody bought, the title or the tool is wrong. Ask one of the five: would you even install this? Then change the title, not the whole stack.

Week 3: teach the failure mode, three times

Three posts or emails that teach one stop rule. Soft link. Example: it asked for the missing amount instead of inventing it. End with $19, ten-minute install, link in bio. If you are not public, send three more personal asks instead. Count: asks, sales, sample-ran, refunds and why. If refunds say wrong model, the listing is the bug.

Week 4: fix, do not expand

Date the README. Rerun the sample if the model moved. Email v1.1 or v1.2 to people who bought. Do not open a membership. Do not add a setup call to the $19. A second skill only if a stranger asked for the next job.

Quality bar

Instructions that survive you leaving the room

Role in one line. Inputs named. Output format named. Three quality checks. A stop rule for missing facts. No be helpful filler. No claim that it replaces a bookkeeper, a lawyer, or a clinician. It drafts. They send.

The sample is real enough to trust

Blur names. Keep the ugly: a client who pays late every time, a line with a missing PO, a note in all caps. If the sample is a perfect table, the skill will look smart and fail on Friday.

Install a tired person can finish

One page. Numbered clicks. One screenshot if a menu is hidden. A line that says you will know it worked when the sample output looks like this. If they have to watch a 12-minute video, you wrote a course. Cut it.

Test 1: the install test

Hand the zip to someone who did not write it. Time them. Under ten minutes to a usable sample output, you passed. If they need you, the one-pager failed.

Test 2: the broken-example test

Missing amount, missing date, rude note. It asks once, then stops. If it guesses, rewrite the stop rule before you advertise.

Test 3: the voice test

If a buyer says it sounds like AI, the instructions need their voice. Add three sample sentences they actually send. Marcus put two real follow-ups he had already mailed (names changed) into SKILL.txt under match this tone. That killed the peppy bot voice.

Test 4: the claims test

No medical, legal, or financial claims. No skill that claims it is compliant. No this will collect the invoice. Operational drafting only. Put the limit in the instructions and on the listing. It drafts. They send.

Test 5: the model-name test

The title names the tool. The install names the clicks for that tool only. If two people refund because they use the other model, the listing failed, not the skill.

Below the bar

Prompts without install steps. A title with no job. A sample that is too clean. Instructions that guess at missing money. A 14-page install. Promising every model. If a tired person cannot run the sample in ten minutes, it is below the bar.

Metrics that matter (and vanity numbers to ignore)

Count these

  • Installs that produce a first output from the sample (ask: Did the sample run?)
  • Stranger sales at $19
  • It broke emails — these are the roadmap
  • Time-to-install reports. If two people say it took 30 minutes, the one-pager failed
  • Refunds because of the wrong model. That is a listing problem. Fix the title.
  • Version number. If v1.0 never becomes v1.1, you are not talking to buyers.

Week 1

Count: instructions written, real example run, broken example run, zip opens, self-buy works, five asks sent. If the broken example still guesses, you do not have a product yet.

Day 30

Count asks, sales, stranger sales, sample-ran answers, break-emails, refunds-reason, version. A healthy day-30: sample runs, 5+ asks, 1+ stranger sale or at least one install without you, 0 to 1 refunds and those are listing problems you already fixed.

Day 90

Count v1.1 shipped (yes/no). Second skill (should still be no, unless a stranger asked for the next job). Cash in the $19 to $39 window, totaled. If you have $0 at day 90, the failure is usually title, unnamed tool, or five asks you did not send. It is rarely the market.

Ignore these

Stars on a prompt marketplace. How many skills you listed. GitHub-style star counts. Views on the screen recording if nobody clicks the checkout. Lines of instructions. Community member counts you do not have yet.

One line a week

Date, asks sent, sales, break-emails, version number, one buyer sentence (did the sample run?). If the buyer sentence is always empty, you are not asking. Ask.

Objections you will hear

I already have a Custom GPT / a Project

Good. This is a better set of instructions plus a sample so they can test it. If theirs already does the job, they should not buy. If they keep tweaking it every week, $19 is the freeze-frame that works.

Skills are going to be free from the labs

Some will be. Generic ones. A client-follow-up skill that knows a solo bookkeeper's tone and will not invent an amount is not on the default home screen. You are selling the job, not the concept of a skill.

I am not technical

Neither is the buyer, if you wrote the install. If you cannot write the install without the word repo, this path will hurt. Use Claude Projects or Custom GPTs, not a local install.

What if the model changes and it breaks

You version the file. You date the README: Tested on Claude, [month year]. You email v1.1 to people who bought. That is the job after the first sale. It is also why you do not sell 40 jobs in one zip — you cannot maintain them.

Can you just set it up for me

Yes, as a service, for a different price. This path is the zip. If you want setup-for-hire, that is Custom project setups or Productized AI service. Do not throw a call into a $19 product.

Can't I just save a prompt

You can. A skill pack is the instructions plus failure modes plus a sample so you know it loaded. If your saved prompt already asks for missing amounts and never invents them, you do not need this. If you rewrite the instructions every Friday, $19 is cheaper than another Friday.

Does it work in ChatGPT / Claude / Gemini

This one is built for [named tool]. I will not pretend it is the same in the other. If you only use the other, do not buy this version. Refund if you already did.

I need it connected to Gmail

That is Automation setups or Custom project setups, priced as a project. Do not promise inbox connection inside a $19 zip.

Is $19 too low if it saves a Friday every week

It is the right first price. Raise to $29 to $39 after a stranger has installed it and you have the screen and the failure modes. Do not start at $79 with no proof.

What if Anthropic or OpenAI ships this exact skill

Then you sell the version that knows this job's tone and failure modes, or you move to the playbook and the service. Generic will always be free later. Specific stays yours if the sample is real.

How this feeds other paths

Upstream: what you need before this

You need a job you have already run in a model more than twice. If you have never run the job, write a playbook or take a service job first, then freeze the instructions from the scars.

Same job, other shapes

The instructions inside the skill are a Niche prompt stack if someone wants to paste instead of install. The sequence you used to build it is Sell an AI playbook. The checklist in the README is an AI template. Let the first buyers tell you which shape they asked for. Do not split until a stranger has installed v1.

Where it gets sold

AI-assisted short-form: the 20-second blank-vs-skill clip is the whole path. A weekly AI letter: one failure mode explained, link to the zip. Your front door: a diagnostic (do you rewrite the same Claude chat every Friday?) then the skill.

When it becomes a service or a membership

Local businesses + AI: install the same skill for a nearby owner and charge a setup fee. Custom project setups and Automation setups are the grown-up version for people who want it connected to their inbox. A small AI membership is how you send v1.2, v1.3 as the model changes — after the $19 file has strangers using it. Do not open a membership to avoid shipping v1.

What not to feed yet

A GPT store listing as the first 72 hours. A catalog of six skills. Thirty days, one job, one tool in the title. After a stranger installs it, the next path is the one they asked for.

Mistakes that kill this path

1. Shipping prompts without install steps

Recovery this week: write the one-page install as clicks. Add it to the zip. Email v1.1.

2. Promising it works on every model

Recovery this week: pick one tool. Put it in the title. Refund anyone who bought the wrong one.

3. Bundling 40 jobs so none of them are good

Recovery this week: ship one job. Archive the rest. One appliance that works beats a store of toys.

4. Using other people's copyrighted prompt packs as your file

Recovery this week: stop listing it. Write the instructions from the job you actually do. The scar tissue is the product.

5. A title with no job

Recovery this week: rename. Client follow-up skill for solo bookkeepers, not Claude Power Pack. Same zip, new title, same $19.

6. A sample that is too clean

Recovery this week: replace it with a messy real week, names blurred. Keep the missing PO and the all-caps note. Rerun. Save as SAMPLE.

7. Instructions that guess at missing money or medical facts

Recovery this week: add the stop rule. Ask once, then stop. Rerun the broken example. Do not ship a silent guesser. Invented numbers, invented legal language, a medical or legal skill that claims it is compliant: delete those claims. This path drafts operational writing. It does not practice. Put that limit in the instructions and on the listing.

8. A 14-page install or a 12-minute video

Recovery this week: cut to one page of clicks. One screenshot if a menu is hidden. Email v1.1.

9. Asking fifty people for features, or naming it after yourself

Recovery this week: stop the survey. Ask five people who already use the model to buy and install. Fix what they trip on. Rename the zip and the checkout after the job: bookkeeper-client-followup-claude-v1.zip.

10. A $97 setup call, or a second skill before a stranger sale

Recovery this week: pull the call out of the $19. If you want setup-for-hire, that is a different path at a different number. Close the other skill draft. Fix the install trip-up on this one. Send five new asks.

Tools and how you actually use them

Where the skill lives

Claude Projects: paste the instructions into the project. Custom GPTs: paste into the GPT builder instructions. Gemini Gems: same idea, different menu. Pick one for v1. Write the install for that one only. You are not shipping an API app. You are shipping text files a human pastes. If you need Zapier, you wandered into Automation setups.

Claude Projects, the actual clicks

Do this yourself before you write INSTALL. Write the clicks from the screen in front of you, not from memory.

  1. Go to claude.ai. Log in. If Projects require Plus or Pro, say so on the listing. Do not sell a Project skill to a free account that cannot see the menu.
  2. Open Projects from the left sidebar on desktop. On mobile, open the menu first.
  3. New Project. Name it the job: Client follow-up.
  4. Find custom instructions / Project instructions. Paste the entire SKILL.txt. Save. Do not paste SKILL into the chat. The chat is for raw material.
  5. Do not upload SAMPLE-INPUT as a project file. Friday is a paste. The first message should still be a paste.
  6. New chat inside the project. Paste SAMPLE-INPUT.txt. Send.
  7. Compare to SAMPLE-OUTPUT.txt. Then paste a real list.

If Projects is not in their plan, do not sell them this zip. Refund. Or ship a Custom GPT version as a separate product after you have clicked it.

Custom GPTs, the actual clicks

Use this when your buyer lives in ChatGPT, not Claude. Do this yourself. Then write INSTALL from the screen.

  1. Go to chatgpt.com. Log in. If creating a GPT requires Plus, say so on the listing.
  2. On the left, GPTs, then Create. Or Explore GPTs, then Create.
  3. Open the Configure tab, not only the chat-based Create tab. You want the Instructions box.
  4. Name: Client follow-up for solo bookkeepers. Description: Paste an invoice list. Get send-ready emails. It will not invent amounts.
  5. Instructions: paste the entire SKILL.txt.
  6. Conversation starters: Paste your invoice list is enough. Do not add cute starters.
  7. Knowledge: you may upload SAMPLE-INPUT.txt and SAMPLE-OUTPUT.txt so they can type run the sample. Still tell them to paste the sample as a message, because Friday is a paste, not a file hunt.
  8. Capabilities: turn off web browsing if the job does not need it. Turn off image generation. This job is text.
  9. Save. Only me while you test. Then Anyone with a link for buyers. You are not putting this in the public GPT store in week one.
  10. Open the GPT. Paste SAMPLE-INPUT. Compare to SAMPLE-OUTPUT. The row with a missing amount must ask.

Your zip still contains SKILL.txt, SAMPLE-INPUT, SAMPLE-OUTPUT, and INSTALL. INSTALL names these clicks. Add a line: if ChatGPT moved the Create button, reply with a screenshot and I will bump INSTALL.

Gemini Gems, if that is where they live

Same idea. Gem instructions get SKILL.txt. First message is the raw list. Write INSTALL only if you actually use Gems for this job. Do not add a Gem appendix from a blog post you have not clicked. If you do not live there, do not sell there.

The zip and the page

Folder: README (the install), SKILL or INSTRUCTIONS, SAMPLE-INPUT, SAMPLE-OUTPUT. Zip it. Stripe Payment Link or Stan delivers the zip. That is the stack. Do not add a course platform.

The 20-second screen

Phone screen record is enough. Desktop is cleaner if the buyer is on desktop. Show the blank chat failing or stalling, then the skill succeeding on the same paste. No intro bumper. The still from second 3 is the thumbnail.

What not to buy

A course platform. A prompt marketplace membership. A local-install stack. Ads. A designer for a thumbnail that hides the job. A second checkout tool. You are selling a $19 zip of text files.

The $0 path

The model you already pay for (or the free tier, if it can hold project instructions). A text editor you already have. Zip from your file manager. Stripe Payment Link (cost per sale). Phone screen record. Five asks to people who already use the model. You do not need a new laptop, a microphone, or a developer account.

Setup order

Write the instructions in a plain file. Run a real example. Run a broken example. Write the one-page install. Zip four files. Create the payment link with that zip. Buy it from a second email. Record 20 seconds. Then ask five people. Do not set up a GPT store before the self-buy works. Do not compare six tools.

Ship checklist

Before you zip

  • One job in the title
  • One tool named (Claude Projects, Custom GPTs, or Gemini Gems)
  • Instructions: role, inputs, output format, quality checks, stop rules
  • Will not invent named fields (amounts, dates, diagnoses)
  • Real sample input and sample output
  • Broken-example test: it asked, then stopped
  • Three sample sentences of their voice, if a buyer would say it sounds like AI
  • One-page install with the actual clicks
  • One screenshot if a menu is hidden
  • Version number on the README
  • Filename after the job, not FINAL_v7
  • Tested-on line with month and year

Before you write INSTALL

  • You have clicked the install yourself this week, on the tool you named
  • The first message after install is only the raw material
  • You know which menu is hidden on mobile
  • You have a line that says you will know it worked when the sample matches SAMPLE-OUTPUT
  • If a step is set up your workspace, rewrite it as a click

Before you ask anyone

  • Zip opens on a phone
  • Checkout title = the job; price $19
  • Tool named on the listing
  • Refund line on the page
  • Self-purchase from a second email
  • 20-second screen recorded
  • Five names who already use the model
  • After-purchase three-line email written
  • No second skill, no 40-job bundle
  • No setup call inside the $19

After the first install

  • Ask: did the sample run?
  • Fix the install trip-up
  • Ship v1.1 to people who bought
  • No second skill until a stranger sale
  • Log: date, asks, sales, break-emails, version

The night you list it

  • Checkout title matches the job
  • Tool is in line one of the listing
  • Link in the five messages is the live link
  • You bought it from a second email on a phone and the zip opened
  • Print the before-you-zip list. If a box is empty, that is tonight's work. Do not start a second SKILL.txt.

FAQ

Is this just a prompt pack?

No. A prompt pack is paste-as-you-go. A skill pack is installed once so the first message can be the raw material. If they want 25 separate prompts for a clinic week, that is Niche prompt stacks. If they want follow-up to live in Claude, that is this.

Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini?

Pick the one you actually use for this job. Write for that one. Saying works everywhere is how you get refunds.

Do I need to code?

No. You need to write instructions and a one-page install. If you are building an API wrapper, you left this path.

What if Anthropic or OpenAI ships this exact skill?

Then you sell the version that knows this job's tone and failure modes, or you move to the playbook and the service. Generic will always be free later. Specific stays yours if the sample is real.

How many skills should I launch with?

One. Five asks. One stranger sale. Then a second skill only if they ask for the next job.

Can I put it on a GPT store or a skill directory?

After it works at $19 on your own checkout. Directories are extra. They are not the first 72 hours.

What do I do when a buyer says it sounds like AI?

The instructions need their voice. Add three sample sentences they actually send. Marcus put two real follow-ups he had already mailed (names changed) into SKILL.txt under match this tone. That killed the peppy bot voice.

Is $19 too low if it saves a Friday every week?

It is the right first price. Raise to $29 to $39 after a stranger has installed it and you have the screen and the failure modes. Do not start at $79 with no proof.

What if they want it connected to Gmail?

That is Automation setups or Custom project setups, priced as a project. Do not promise inbox connection inside a $19 zip.

Can I use someone else's skill as a base?

No. Do not use other people's copyrighted prompt packs as your file. Write the instructions from the job you actually do. The scar tissue is the product.

What do I do after five asks and zero sales?

Ask one of the five: would you even install this? Then look at the title and the tool name. Most first misses are a vibe title or a missing tool. Rewrite. Send five new asks. Do not rewrite the whole skill yet.

Should I include a setup call at $19?

No. That is a service. Keep the zip at $19. If you want to get paid for your time this week, use Productized AI service or Custom project setups.

How do I know the install is done?

A person who did not write it can finish it in under ten minutes and get a usable first output from the sample. Time someone. If they need you, add a screenshot. If they need a video, you overbuilt.

When do I bump the version?

When you fix install wording, add a screenshot, or change a stop rule. Put v1.1 in the README and the filename. Email people who already bought. Same checkout, new zip.

What if the buyer wants a ChatGPT version of my Claude skill?

That is a second product, after a stranger has installed this one. Do not pretend they are the same. If you build it, name the tool in the title and test it on that tool. Do not copy-paste the install clicks.

Do I need a landing page?

No. A Payment Link or Stan page whose title is the job is enough. A simple page that repeats the listing body is fine. Do not build a site instead of sending five asks.

What this actually is

Definition

A niche prompt stack is 25 prompts that finish a repeating writing job for one trade. Not 1,000 clever one-liners. Not a course. Not a model. Each prompt is a form: the buyer pastes named inputs, gets a named output in a named format, and has a one-line done check so they know it is sendable. The stack covers a month of that trade's weekly writing: texts, emails, captions, listings, lesson notes, reminders. The buyer is not collecting prompts. They are trying to get through this week's writing without sounding like a robot or saying the wrong thing.

Twenty-five that finish a job beat a thousand that sound clever. A clinic front desk with 14 reminder texts before lunch does not want a vault. They want the vocabulary of their trade, the lines that trade will not cross, and the format that actually gets sent.

What this is not

You are not selling medical, legal, or financial advice. You are not selling a promise that a model is HIPAA compliant, court ready, or tax-safe. You are not selling access to ChatGPT. They already have a tab open. You are selling writing help for repeating operational jobs, with the constraints a practitioner already lives with.

You are not selling a thousand-prompt dump titled Ultimate AI Prompt Vault. That market is dead and noisy. A stack for pediatric clinic SMS that stays human and avoids diagnosis language does not exist for free.

You are not selling a skill pack. A skill pack is installed so the first message is raw material. A prompt stack is paste-as-you-go.

Why it works now

Generic prompt packs became free the week models got good at sounding helpful. The remaining gap is not "how do I talk to a model." It is "how do I talk to this model about this job without violating the rules of this room." That gap is vocabulary, constraints, and format. Those live in a trade, not in a prompt marketplace.

Models still ramble. They still invent a follow-up plan. They still put another child's name in a waitlist text. They still write a 90-word SMS. The stack is the freeze of the instructions a careful person would type every time, if they had 20 extra minutes, which they do not. Search is specific now. People type "pediatric clinic reminder text." Title-match is the distribution. Niche is the moat.

Anti-pattern 1: the thousand-prompt dump

A zip of 1,000 prompts with no inputs, no format, and no done check is a toy. You cannot date-test 1,000. Sell 25 you have actually run.

Anti-pattern 2: clever prompts that do not match the job

A prompt that returns a three-paragraph waitlist email for a clinic that only sends SMS is a mismatch. A prompt that names another patient in a cancellation text is a liability. Sit with a practitioner. Match length, channel, and the never-say list. If you cannot name those from the inside, you have a costume.

Anti-pattern 3: compliance theater

"HIPAA-compliant prompts." "Court-ready language." "IRS-safe emails." Those phrases sell to scared people and then produce refunds. No pack of prompts is a compliance program. Operational writing around regulated fields can be fine: appointment SMS, not treatment plans; listing descriptions, not contract clauses. Know the line and print it on page one.

The deal you keep

You keep three promises. One: every prompt has inputs, output format, a hard constraint, and a done check. Two: you have run all 25 on realistic inputs and kept three before/after proofs with names blurred. Three: you will not claim compliance, diagnosis, legal outcomes, or financial results. The buyer keeps one promise in return: they will paste real inputs and send the result. You design for that first paste. If prompt 1 does not survive a Friday afternoon, the stack is not a product.

Who this is for — and who should skip it

Fits if

You know a trade or hobby from the inside: realtors, tutors, gyms, writers, clinics, bookkeepers, wedding photographers, salon owners. You have sat in the job long enough to list the ten writing tasks people hate. You can tell a good reminder from a creepy one. You already belong to a group or forum where those people talk, and you have helped in that room without pitching. You do not need a huge audience. You need the niche word they would search, and enough respect in that room to share once without getting banned. You can write a constraint in one line: "I will not diagnose. I will not name another patient."

Skip if

Skip if your only edge is "I use ChatGPT a lot." Skip if you planned to copy someone else's stack and swap the niche word. Skip if you want to write for "everyone who uses AI." Skip medical, legal, or financial claims. Operational writing around those fields can be fine (appointment SMS, not treatment plans). Skip if you have never sent the kind of message the stack produces. Skip if you need money tomorrow — first stranger sale is often day 8 to day 14. Take a productized service job first if you need cash this week.

The honest middle

You do not have to be the owner. Front desk, assistant, listing coordinator, tutor who also runs the parent emails: that is enough inside knowledge. You do have to sit with a practitioner for an hour if that practitioner is not you. Take notes on the jobs they hate, the channel, the length, and the never-say list. Then write. Do not invent the never-say list from a blog post.

You are not waiting to become famous in the niche. You are waiting to have 25 forms that match how the week actually runs.

Skills and time

You need the niche vocabulary, a four-part form, a PDF export, a checkout, and the willingness to ask once in a room you already belong to. You do not need design, a certificate, or a following. Time if you already know the jobs: two evenings to list, three to write and run 25, one for SOP and proofs, one for checkout and ten shares. That is the 5 to 14 day window. If you do not know the jobs, research first. Do not spend 72 hours guessing a clinic week.

Two-minute self-test

Answer these out loud. If you stall on two of them, this is not your first path this month.

  • What is the niche word they would type into search?
  • What are five writing jobs that happen every week in that trade?
  • What channel is each job (SMS, email, listing, caption)?
  • What is one thing you must never say in that room?
  • Where is a group you already belong to, where a helpful comment would not get you banned?
  • Can you run 25 prompts this week on realistic inputs and keep three before/afters with names blurred?

If you have the niche word, the five jobs, the never-say line, and a room, start. If you only have "I like prompts," go do a job in a trade first.

The buyer on the other side

A niche buyer who uses the first prompt the same day. They have a shift or a showing tomorrow. They will paste one input and send one message. They are tired and slightly scared of sounding cold or saying the wrong thing. They will pay $19 to freeze the instructions they keep retyping.

The offer, named in one sentence

Fill this before you outline

"I help [niche person] write [repeating job] every week with 25 prompts that include inputs, output format, and a done check, even if they hate sounding like a robot."

If you cannot fill the brackets, you do not have a stack. Niche person is a job plus a setting: pediatric clinic front desk, not "healthcare." Repeating job is the week's writing, named. The even-if is the honest fear: sounding cold, saying the wrong medical thing, writing a brochure.

Title includes the niche word they would search. "25 prompts for pediatric clinic SMS and emails" is searchable. "Ultimate AI Prompt Vault" is not.

Five sentences that already work

  • I help pediatric clinic staff write the week's SMS and parent emails in 25 prompts with inputs, format, and a done check, even if they are scared of sounding cold or of saying the wrong medical thing.
  • I help solo realtors write listing descriptions and showing follow-ups in 25 prompts, even if they only have MLS notes and 15 minutes in the car.
  • I help independent tutors write parent updates and lesson recaps in 25 prompts, even if they freeze on tone and never know how honest to be about a rough week.
  • I help small gym owners write class reminder texts, no-show follow-ups, and intro-offer captions in 25 prompts, even if they hate sounding like a used-car ad.
  • I help wedding photographers write inquiry replies, timeline emails, and gallery-delivery notes in 25 prompts, even if they only want to be behind the camera.

Write yours in that shape. One person. One repeating job. 25 prompts. One fear.

What they get

A PDF or a Notion doc. Twenty-five prompts covering a month of the weekly jobs. Each prompt has named inputs, output format including length, a hard "I will not" constraint, and a one-line done check. A one-page SOP: which prompt when, mapped to a real week. Three before/after examples, names blurred, texture kept. A dated line on page one: "Tested on [model], [month year]." Price $12 to $29. Default $19.

They get the vocabulary and the constraints, in an order that matches a real week. They get a second-pass polish prompt paired with each draft family.

What they do not get

A thousand prompts. A claim of compliance. A community. A new model. A Zoom setup call. A custom version inside their SMS tool. A HIPAA certificate. Lifetime updates you will not ship. A second niche thrown in "for value."

If they want the stack installed as a Claude Project, that is Ship a Claude or ChatGPT skill pack, after this file has been used. If they want you to sit with their clinic and write their 25, that is a productized service. Do not hide a service inside a $19 PDF.

Packaging

One file. One title with the niche word. One price on the page. Cover: title, who it is for, what it will not do, tested-on date. Then the SOP, the 25 numbered prompts, the three proofs. Export PDF. If you use Notion, include a duplicate-this link and a PDF backup.

Do not ship a zip of 25 separate files. Copy-paste blocks that are the whole prompt. Week 4, if they ask: add a one-page weekly calendar and raise to $29, or keep $19 and add the extra page. Do not invent a $49 "pro vault" with the same 25 prompts in a different font.

What "done" looks like

Definition

Done is a stranger in that trade who pastes prompt 1 the same day, sends the result, and does not email you to ask what to do next. The file is 25 complete prompts, a one-page SOP, three proofs, a dated test line, a niche-word title, and a working $19 checkout you have bought from a second email. Done is not five marketplace listings and a brand name. If a prompt is clever but would never be sent in that trade, it is not done. Cut it.

Fairness test

Would you sell this to a tired friend who does that job, at $19, without a speech? If you would discount it or offer a call to "walk them through," it is not fair yet. Fair means they can open prompt 3 at 9 p.m., paste four fields, and send. Fair also means you have not claimed compliance. If they say "we would never send the after," rewrite the prompt, not the screenshot.

Technical done

Twenty-five prompts. Each has inputs, output format, a constraint ("I will not..."), and a done check. A one-page SOP that maps the week: Monday reminder, Tuesday waitlist, and so on. Three before/after pairs from realistic inputs. A dated line: "Tested on [model], [month year]." Page one states the limit: operational writing only, no medical, legal, or financial claims.

You have run all 25 on real or realistic inputs. Names blurred. Texture kept: the short-notice cancellation, the parent who texts at 9 p.m., the price question you are allowed to answer. Checkout title matches the file title. Self-purchase delivers the PDF.

Not-done-yet list

  • A title without the niche word
  • Prompts that are slogans ("write a friendly reminder")
  • Prompts with no length or channel
  • No "I will not" line
  • No done check
  • You have not run all 25
  • Before/afters that are fake-clean or leak a real name
  • A compliance claim on the cover or in the listing
  • Checkout untested
  • SOP missing, so they have 25 orphans
  • You have not asked once, helpfully, in a room you already belong to
  • A second niche started before a stranger used prompt 1

If three of those are true, you have a draft. Keep going. Do not list a draft and "improve it with feedback." The first buyer is not your editor.

Pricing that holds

Ranges

$12 is for a tiny stack: 10 prompts, one job, one channel. $19 is the home price for 25 prompts plus SOP plus three proofs. $29 is fair if you add a one-page weekly calendar they asked for, or a second-language polish pass that a bilingual staffer still checks. Stay in the $12 to $29 window. This is not a $97 course.

Default to $19. Put it on the page. Do not "DM for price." Do not do $9 to "beat Etsy." A $9 file trains people to treat you like a free list. Race to a title that matches search and a first prompt they can use today, not to the bottom of the marketplace.

When to raise

Raise after a stranger has used a prompt the same day and you have added something they asked for. Then move $19 to $29. Raise because the file does more, not because you got bored. Add one page, not five bonuses. Do not invent a $49 "pro vault" with the same 25 prompts in a different font.

Refunds in one sentence

If it is not useful, or if you bought thinking this was a compliance or legal product, email me and I will refund.

You will refund almost nobody if prompt 1 works and page one states the limit. Refund the HIPAA-seeker fast and without a speech. Then make the listing clearer.

Never charge for these

Never charge for a compliance certificate you cannot issue. Never charge extra for "lifetime updates" you will not ship. Never charge for a setup call inside the $19. Never charge $97 for 25 prompts. Never charge a second time for v1.1 when the model moved; email it if you have their address.

Worked dollars

Priya sells the clinic stack at $19. Ten personal shares. Two group buys in week 1: $38. A stranger on day 10 from title search: $19. Three more in week 3: $57. One HIPAA-seeker refund: minus $19. Week 4 she adds the calendar after they ask, raises new sales to $29, emails the calendar free to people who already paid $19. Month 1 cash is about $180 after the refund. That is the path. Not a launch. A searchable tool.

The first 72 hours

Day 1 morning: list the jobs

Sit with a practitioner, even if it is you. Write the ten repeating writing jobs in that niche. Do not open a model yet. Star the five that happen every week. Those five become the spine of the 25. If you cannot name ten, you do not have 72 hours. You have research. Call someone who does the job. Ask: what do you write every Monday, what do you send when someone cancels, what are you not allowed to say, what length actually gets sent. Leave annual jobs for a later stack.

Day 1 afternoon: write the first family

Write five prompts for the first starred job. Each prompt is a form. Paste this to draft, then rewrite it in the trade's voice:

Write a prompt for [person] who has to [job] every week. The prompt must have: (1) inputs they paste, named; (2) output format, including length; (3) a hard constraint of what it will not say; (4) a done check in one line. Kitchen-table English. No hype. No medical, legal, or financial claims.

Then rewrite every line as if you will never be in the room. Name the fields. Name the character count. Name the never-say. Name the send test. Start with the Friday-afternoon ones: reminders, no-shows, short-notice cancellations.

Day 1 night: run those five

Paste realistic inputs. Fake names. Real rhythms: a parent texting at 9 p.m., a sibling double-book, an interpreter need. If you would not send the output, rewrite the prompt, not the output. Save the best before (generic dump) and after (your prompt, sendable). Stop at midnight. You have five, not 25. That is a good day.

Day 2: the other four families

Morning: five prompts for schedule changes. Afternoon: five for after-visit admin. Evening: five for allowed FAQs, plus five polish passes (shorten to 160, warmer without cute, cut diagnosis language, second-language draft to be checked, done-check against the never-say list). Run as you go. Keep a column: prompt number, ran, sendable, rewrite note.

Day 3: SOP, proofs, title, checkout, one ask

Morning: write the one-page SOP. A table: day or trigger, job, prompt number, where it gets sent. Pull the three best before/after pairs. Blur names. Keep texture. Put "Tested on [model], [month year]" on page one with the limit line.

Afternoon: export PDF. Title includes the niche word. "25 prompts for pediatric clinic SMS and parent emails — inputs, format, done check." Price $19. Stripe Payment Link, Etsy, or Stan. Test-buy from a second email. Open the file.

Night: one helpful ask in a group you already belong to. Answer someone's actual question with a useful line, then mention the file once in your profile or in a comment if the group allows it. Also send five personal messages to people who do the job. Do not open a second niche. Do not wait until Monday.

The path, step by step

Step 1. Sit with a practitioner and list the hated jobs

Even if the practitioner is you. Write the jobs they hate writing. Ten of them. Use their words: "the no-show text I never send because I sound mad," not "customer retention." If you are not the practitioner, pay for 30 minutes and record the list, the channel, the length, and the never-say list. Inside knowledge is the only moat this product has. Without it you will write clever prompts that do not match the job.

Step 2. Star the five that happen every week

Those five become the spine of the 25. Five jobs times five prompts each is a month of work, including variants: 24-hour vs same-day, SMS vs email, one child vs sibling. Do not spend the 25 on annual jobs. Weekly is what they will use the same day, which is how this path defines a first sale.

Step 3. Write each prompt as a four-part form

"Paste [named fields]. I will return [output] in [format and length]. I will not [constraint]. Done when [send test]." If you cannot fill those blanks, you do not have a prompt. You have a slogan. "Write a reminder text" is free and useless. "Paste parent first name, child first name, appointment day, appointment time, clinic phone. Return one SMS under 160 characters. No diagnosis language. No 'just checking in.' Done when a tired parent could tap send." is a product.

Step 4. Pair a second-pass polish prompt with each draft family

"Tighten this. Keep the facts. Cut the fluff. Stay under 160 characters. Do not add cute warmth. Do not add a diagnosis." Pair it with the draft so they are not stuck with a first-pass robot paragraph. One polish prompt can serve a whole family.

Step 5. Run all 25 on realistic inputs

Fake names. Real rhythms. Save outputs. If you would not send it, rewrite the prompt, not the output. The product is the prompt that produces sendable work, not a hand-edited miracle. Skipping the run-through is how you discover a bad prompt after a refund.

Step 6. Keep three before/after proofs and blur the names

Before is what they would have sent, or a generic dump of the same inputs. After is what your prompt produced, sendable with little edit — if you had to heavily edit, the prompt is not done. Names blurred. Texture kept. Do not invent clinical advice. Do not scrape a clinic's real SMS. Put the three proofs in the file, not only on the sales page.

Step 7. Date the tests on page one

"Tested on [model], [month year]." Put it on page one and next to the three proofs. Models move. If the date is six months old, run the 25 again before you advertise. This is why you sell 25 for one niche, not 1,000 for everyone.

Step 8. Write the one-page SOP

A table: day or trigger, job, prompt number, channel. Monday 24-hour reminders: prompt 1, SMS. Tuesday waitlist: prompt 6, SMS. This is the difference between a pile and a stack. Write the SOP before they ask.

Step 9. Put it in a PDF (or Notion plus a PDF backup)

PDF is simpler for Stripe and Etsy. Notion is fine with a duplicate-this link and a PDF backup. Copy-paste blocks that are the whole prompt. Numbered headings. Cover page: title with niche word, who it is for, what it will not do, tested-on date, reply-to. No twelve-page brand story.

Step 10. Title includes the niche word they would search

"25 prompts for pediatric clinic SMS and parent emails — inputs, format, done check." Not "AI magic for healthcare creators." Put the niche word first. Put the job. Put "prompts." Generic "ChatGPT prompts" on Etsy is a graveyard. "Pediatric clinic SMS prompts" is a search.

Step 11. Checkout, then buy it yourself

Stripe Payment Link, Etsy, or Stan. Sell on your site first. Marketplace second if the titles match search. One product, one price, one file. Test-buy from a second email, on a phone. Open the PDF. Put the refund line on the page. Put the limit line on the page. If the page is a menu of six ideas, cut it back to this stack.

Step 12. Ten personal shares, help first

DMs to people who do the job. One helpful comment in a group you already belong to, once. One post with the niche word. Help first: answer someone's actual question with a useful line, then mention the file once in your profile if the group allows it. Not a dump of 25 prompts in the thread. First sale can be someone you know who does the job. Ask what they used.

Step 13. Ask the first buyer which prompt they used the same day

That prompt becomes your public example. If they tripped, fix that prompt the same week and send v1.1. One used prompt is worth more than a redesign. Put their (blurred, permitted) line on the sales page: "Used prompt 3, same-day reminder, the afternoon I bought it."

Step 14. Only add a calendar or a second stack if they ask

Do not copy someone else's stack and swap the niche word. If two buyers ask "which one on Monday," you needed the SOP or the calendar. Add that page. If nobody asks for a realtor version, do not build a realtor version. Depth in one niche beats a catalog of costumes.

Step 15. Rerun when the model moves

When the model changes, run the 25 again, starting with the three proofs. If they break, fix the prompts, bump the date, email buyers if you have their addresses. The dated line is a promise. Keeping it is how a $19 file earns a $29 bundle later.

Step 16. Stop

Do not add a community. Do not add a $97 course of you reading the 25. Do not open five Etsy listings with synonym titles. One stack, one title, one price, one room. When a stranger has used prompt 1 the same day, you may consider the skill-pack version of the best five. Not before.

A worked example

Priya, pediatric clinic SMS and emails, $19

Priya has worked the front desk of a pediatric clinic. She knows the week: reminder texts, waitlist offers, cancellation messages, after-visit thank-yous, no-show follow-ups, form reminders, weather closures, and the portal redirect. She does not write treatment advice. She writes the operational messages parents actually need.

On a Sunday in March she writes the one sentence: "I help pediatric clinic staff write the week's SMS and emails in 25 prompts with inputs, format, and a done check, even if they are scared of sounding cold or of saying the wrong medical thing." File: "25 prompts for pediatric clinic SMS and parent emails." Price: $19. Format: PDF plus a one-page SOP.

Calendar: days 1 to 14

Day 1: she lists ten jobs and stars five. Days 2 to 4: she writes and runs 25. Eleven first drafts fail sendable: too long, too cute, or they invent a follow-up plan. She rewrites those eleven. Day 5: SOP and three proofs. Day 6: PDF, Stripe Payment Link, self-buy. Day 7: she answers a clinic-managers Facebook thread about no-show texts with two principles (no shame, one next step, no clinical content), then links her profile. She DMs five people she has worked with.

Day 8: two people from the group buy. $38. She asks which prompt they used today. One says prompt 3, same-day reminder. Day 10: a stranger finds the listing because the title matched "pediatric clinic SMS." $19. First stranger sale. Prompt 3 becomes the public example.

What the 25 cover

Five weekly jobs, five prompts each: appointment reminders, schedule changes, after-visit admin, front-desk FAQs the clinic is allowed to answer, and polish passes (shorten to 160, warmer without cute, Spanish draft to be checked, cut diagnosis language, never-say check). Every prompt starts with Paste: [fields]. Every prompt ends with Done when: [send test]. Every prompt includes I will not: diagnose, guess a result, promise a clinical outcome, or scold a parent.

The three proofs she kept

A reminder that sounded like a bill collector — generic model output, 52 words, "per our records you have failed to confirm." After: 21 words, child first name, time, clinic phone, no shame. A waitlist text that leaked another child's name — her first prompt draft allowed "another family cancelled." After: the prompt forbids extra names. "A time opened on Thursday at 3:30. Reply YES if you want it." A thank-you email that invented a follow-up plan. After: the prompt forbids plans. Those three are why someone trusts the file.

The mistake and the recovery

On day 9 a buyer emails: "Prompt 11 (forms still due) told a parent the visit could not be completed if forms were missing. That is not true and it scared them." Priya had over-constrained the done check into a threat. She rewrites prompt 11 the same night: facts, one next step, no consequence she cannot stand behind. She emails v1.1 to both buyers. She adds a line on page one: "I will not invent a clinic policy." She dates the PDF "tested March 2026."

A fourth email arrives on day 12: "Is this HIPAA compliant?" She refunds $19 with the sentence from the listing: no pack of prompts is a compliance program. She bolds that sentence on the page. That refund is a listing problem, not a product problem.

First stranger sale, dollars, shipped artifact

Shipped artifact: a 19-page PDF, SOP on page 2, prompts 1 to 25, three before/afters, tested-on line, reply-to on the last page. Month 1: six sales at $19, one refund, two people later buy the $29 calendar bundle she adds in week 4 after they ask which prompt on Monday. Net about $133 plus the two $29s in week 4. Not a launch. A searchable tool. She does not start a realtor stack. She asks every buyer which prompt they used the same day, and prompt 3 stays the public example.

Week-by-week if you have a job

Assume evenings. This is four weeks to a used stack, not a prompt brand.

Week 1: 25 prompts and three proofs

Monday: list ten jobs, star five. Call a practitioner if the list is thin.

Tuesday through Saturday: write and run five prompts a night. Rewrite failures. Saturday night you should have 25 run. If you have 18, use Sunday. Do not list 18.

Sunday: three before/afters, names blurred, SOP table drafted. A prompt you have not run is a guess.

Week 2: listing live, ten personal shares

Monday: cover page, limit line, tested-on date, export PDF. Title with the niche word.

Tuesday: checkout. Self-purchase from a second email on your phone. Fix the download if it fails. Price $19.

Wednesday: five DMs to people who do the job. Help first. Link last.

Thursday: one helpful group comment, once, in a room you already belong to. Profile link, not a thread dump.

Friday: one public post with the niche word and the $19.

Saturday: ask anyone who bought which prompt they used. Fix what they tripped on the same day.

Sunday: ten shares should be done. If they are not, send the remaining DMs. Do not redesign the cover instead. First sale can be someone you know who does the job.

Week 3: SOP in their hands, no second niche

If buyers ask "which one do I use on Monday," you needed the SOP. Add the one-page which-prompt-when if it was thin. Email it to people who already bought. Do not start a second niche. Repeat the public example of the prompt they used first. Rerun any prompt that produced a scared or illegal-sounding line. Count: shares, sales, prompt-used-first, refunds and why. If refunds say "I thought this was HIPAA," the listing is the bug.

Week 4: bundle only if they ask

A calendar or checklist if they ask for it. $19 stays for the original, or $29 for the bundle. Email the extra page free to people who already paid $19. Update the "tested on [month year]" line if the model moved. Do not copy someone else's stack and swap the niche word. If nobody asked, keep $19 and keep sharing the one title. Plan a second stack only after a stranger has used prompt 1 the same day.

Quality bar

Below the bar

A clever one-liner. A prompt with no inputs. A paragraph returned for an SMS channel. Extra names in a waitlist text. Diagnosis language. Shame. A title without the niche word. Fake-clean before/afters. A thousand-prompt dump. "HIPAA compliant." A prompt you have not run. If a tired parent cannot paste and send, it is below the bar.

Above the bar

Paste [x]. I will return [y] in [format]. I will not [constraint]. Done when [check]. Length matches the channel. The after is sendable with little or no hand edit. Names blurred. Dated test. SOP maps the week. Page one states the limit. The first prompt survives a Friday afternoon. Sendable is not optional.

Test 1: the form test

Every prompt has the four parts. Open the PDF at a random page. If you land on a slogan, it fails. Fix that prompt before you advertise.

Test 2: the job-match test

Sit with a practitioner. If clinics send SMS under 160 characters, do not return a paragraph. If they are not allowed to name another patient, the prompt forbids extra names. If listings cannot invent granite counters, the prompt forbids invented finishes. Clever prompts that do not match the job are a listed mistake.

Test 3: the send test

Run it on realistic inputs. Would you send it? If you have to rewrite the output every time, the prompt is the product to fix. Do not ship a hand-edited miracle.

Test 4: the claims test

No medical, legal, or financial claims. No "HIPAA compliant prompts." No "this will win your case." Operational writing only. Put the limit on page one and in every clinical-adjacent prompt: "I will not diagnose, guess a result, or tell a parent to skip a visit."

Test 5: the same-day test

A buyer uses prompt 1 the same day without emailing you. That is the quality bar this path names. If they email "which one do I start with," the SOP failed. If they email "this sounds like a bill collector," prompt 1 failed. Fix this week, not in a v2 you never ship.

Metrics that matter (and vanity numbers to ignore)

Week 1

Count jobs listed, prompts written, prompts run, proofs kept (target 3), SOP exists, checkout self-buy works. If prompts run is less than 25, you do not have a product yet.

Day 30

Count personal shares (target 10 in week 2, then a few each week). Sales. Stranger sales as a subset. Which prompt number they used first. Refunds, with a one-word reason (compliance, mismatch, never-opened). Prompts that failed the run-through and got rewritten. Tested-on date. A healthy day-30: 25 run, 3 proofs, 10+ shares, 1+ stranger sale or at least one same-day use, 0 to 1 refunds and those are listing problems you already fixed.

Day 90

Count v1.1 shipped (yes/no). Calendar added only if asked. Second niche (should still be no, unless a stranger asked and you have a new inside source). Repeat buyers of the $29 bundle. Which five prompts account for most "used first" answers — those five are the skill-pack candidates. Cash in the $12 to $29 window, totaled. If you have $0 at day 90, the failure is usually title, unrun prompts, or shares you did not send. It is rarely "the market."

Ignore these

Prompt count above 25. Etsy hearts. "1,000 prompts" as a flex. Downloads of a free 5-prompt teaser that never converts. Page views from people searching "free ChatGPT prompts." Likes on a post that did not name the niche word. A competitor's vault size. Your own urge to add a community.

One-line spreadsheet

Columns: date, shares, sales, stranger sales, prompt-used-first, refunds-reason, tested-on date, notes (rewrite which #). One row a week. If the tested-on date is six months old, run the 25 again before you advertise. If prompt-used-first is always empty, you are not asking. Ask. That number is how you choose the public example and how you know the stack is a tool, not a collectible.

Objections you will hear

"There are free prompt lists everywhere."

Yes. Generic ones. This stack is the vocabulary and constraints for [niche]. If a free list already has your "I will not" line and your done check, use the free list. If it writes a paragraph a parent will not send, $19 is the niche version.

"Is this HIPAA / legally safe?"

No prompt pack is a compliance program. These are writing aids for operational messages. Clinic policy still applies. I will refund you if you bought thinking this was a legal product. It is not. I will not sell you a "HIPAA prompt." If you need a compliance vendor, that is a different purchase.

"Can't I write my own prompts?"

You can. You are paying for 25 that already ran on realistic inputs, with before/afters, and a SOP for which to use when. If you like writing prompts, write them. If you have a clinic week to get through, buy the stack.

"Will they still work next month?"

Models move. The file is dated. When they move, I run the 25 again and send v1.1. That is why I sell 25 for one niche, not 1,000 for everyone.

"Can you add clinical advice prompts?"

No. Operational writing only. That is a hard line on this path. If they need clinical content, they need a clinician, not a $19 PDF.

"I already have ChatGPT."

Good. These prompts are the constraints and the vocabulary for [niche], not a new model. If your current prompt already refuses extra names, diagnosis language, and 200-character rambling, you do not need this. If you rewrite the instructions every time, $19 is the freeze.

"Why would I pay $19 when Etsy has a 500-prompt pack for $8?"

Because you will not send 500. You will send this week's reminder. Mine is 25, run, with a SOP and three proofs, for one job. The $8 pack is a toy. I will refund you if you open prompt 1 and it is not sendable.

"Can you make one for every kind of clinic?"

No. Pediatric front desk is the file. Urgent care is a different never-say list. Do not buy this and search-replace.

"I need you to install this in our SMS tool."

That is a custom project, not this $19 PDF. If you want it inside a tool, that is a billed setup. I will not hide that inside the checkout.

"My manager will not let us use AI."

Then do not buy this. I am not a policy workaround. If they allow drafting with a human send, this is a draft aid.

How this feeds other paths

Upstream: what you need before this

You need inside knowledge of a trade, or a paid hour with someone who has it. If you have never finished the messages, take a productized service job first, then write the stack from the scars.

Downstream: products that are the same job in another shape

The SOP and the sequence become Sell an AI playbook. The installed version of the best five prompts becomes Ship a Claude or ChatGPT skill pack. The calendar becomes AI templates and SOPs. Do not split until a stranger has used prompt one the same day. Live drops: a dated zip when the model changes. Your front door: "which of these five weekly jobs hurts" then the stack. A weekly AI letter: one prompt taught, link to the 25.

Where the before/afters go

AI-assisted short-form: one before/after per video. End card: the file is $19, link in bio. Do not explain the other 24 in 20 seconds. Teach prompt 3. Sell the stack.

Services, carefully

Local businesses + AI and Productized AI service: sit with one clinic, write their 25, charge a project fee, then productize the generic version with names removed. Custom setups if they want it inside their SMS tool. Do not promise that inside the $19 PDF. If a reply says "can you just do this for us," send a price or send the cheaper file.

What not to feed yet

A membership. A 200-prompt vault. Thirty days, one stack, one niche word. After a stranger uses it, the next path is the one they asked for.

Mistakes that kill this path

1. Clever prompts that do not match the job

Recovery this week: sit with a practitioner for 30 minutes. Rewrite any prompt that returns the wrong channel or length. Cut the clever one-liners.

2. Medical, legal, or financial claims

Recovery this week: delete the claims from the cover, the listing, and every prompt. Add the limit line on page one. Refund anyone who bought for compliance.

3. Copying someone else's stack and swapping the niche word

Recovery this week: stop listing it. Write from the inside or skip the niche. A costume stack produces refunds and a reputation you will not repair with a new cover.

4. A title without the niche word

Recovery this week: rename. "25 prompts for pediatric clinic SMS" not "AI magic pack." Same file, new title, same $19.

5. Prompts with no done check

Recovery this week: add "Done when [send test]" to all 25. Rerun three. Export. Email v1.1.

6. Skipping the run-through

Recovery this week: run all 25 on realistic inputs before you send another share. Rewrite failures. Do not discover a bad prompt after a refund.

7. Before/afters that are fake-clean or leaked

Recovery this week: reconstruct with fake names. Keep texture. Never put another child's name in a waitlist example. Never scrape a clinic's real SMS.

8. A thousand-prompt dump to "look like value"

Recovery this week: ship 25. Archive the rest. Value is sendable, not countable.

9. Selling to "entrepreneurs"

Recovery this week: pick a trade. Put that word in the title. Share in that room. Entrepreneurs buy vaults and do not send texts.

10. Promising HIPAA, court, or tax outcomes

Recovery this week: same as claims. Refund. Clarify. Do not argue in the review.

11. Starting a second niche before a same-day use

Recovery this week: close the other draft. Ask the people who already bought which prompt they used. Fix that one.

12. Dumping 25 prompts in a Facebook thread

Recovery this week: delete if you can. Help in the next thread with two principles and a profile link. Do not fight mods.

Ethics, restated

Do not put another child's name in a waitlist example. Do not invent clinical advice to make a proof dramatic. Do not scrape a clinic's real SMS. Blur, reconstruct, respect the room.

Tools and how you actually use them

Exact stack

A Google Doc or Word file while you draft. Export to PDF. Notion only if your buyer already lives there, plus a PDF backup. One model tab you already pay for. Stripe Payment Link, Etsy, or Stan. A second email for the test-buy. A sheet: prompt number, ran, sendable, rewrite. Do not add a prompt marketplace account in week one.

Setup order

Open a doc. Title with the niche word. Page one: who, limit, tested-on date (fill the date after the run). Write the SOP table as a skeleton. Write prompts 1 to 25 as forms. Run them in the model you will name on page one. Paste proofs. Export PDF. Create the payment link with that PDF. Buy it from the second email. Then share. Do not set up Etsy before the self-buy works. Do not buy a prompt-management app.

What not to buy

A prompt marketplace membership. A "1,000 viral prompts" pack to reskin. A HIPAA course so you can claim compliance. A designer for a cover that hides the niche word. Ads. A second checkout tool. A community platform. A course platform. You are selling a $19 PDF.

The $0 path

Docs or Word you already have. A model free tier is enough to run 25 if you already use one. Checkout: Stripe Payment Link (cost per sale) or Etsy if you already have an account. Export PDF from Docs. Share in a group you already belong to. You do not need Notion or a new phone.

How you run the 25

One sitting per job family. Paste realistic inputs. Save the output. If you would not send it, rewrite the prompt, not the output. Dated tests: page one gets the model name and month. When the model changes, rerun the three proofs first. If they break, fix, bump the date, email buyers if you have their addresses. Filename: "pediatric-clinic-sms-prompts.pdf" not "FINAL_v7." Reply-to on the last page.

Ship checklist

Print this. Tick it. Do not list until the file half is honest.

  • No invented clinical, legal, or financial advice in proofs

  • Limit line on page one: no medical, legal, or financial claims

Before you share

  • Self-purchase works from a second email on a phone
  • PDF opens

After the first use

  • Asked which prompt they used the same day
  • That prompt is the public example
  • Fixed anything they tripped on, same week
  • v1.1 dated if you changed more than a typo

FAQ

Why 25? Why not 100?

Twenty-five that finish a month of weekly jobs beat 100 clever orphans. If you have more, you probably have a second stack. Sell this one first. Default: 25, five families of five.

PDF or Notion?

Either. PDF for Stripe and Etsy. Notion if your buyer already lives there. Include the three proofs in both cases, and a PDF backup if you use Notion. Default: PDF.

Can I sell on Etsy in week one?

You can. Site first is cleaner so you can email v1.1. Etsy second if the title matches search. Default: site first.

What if I am not in that trade?

Sit with a practitioner or skip the niche. Swapping the niche word on someone else's stack is a listed mistake and it produces prompts that do not match the job. Default: skip the niche you have not sat in.

Can I include clinical or legal language?

No. Operational writing only. No medical, legal, or financial claims. If Priya's clinic stack starts drafting treatment plans, she cut those prompts. Appointment SMS, not care. Default: cut it.

Do I need before/afters on the sales page?

Yes. Three. Blur names. Keep the texture. They are the reason a stranger believes this is not another free list. Default: three in the file and at least one on the page.

$12 or $19?

$19 for 25 plus SOP plus proofs. $12 if you only have one job and ten prompts. $29 if they asked for the calendar. Stay in $12 to $29. Default: $19.

What do I do when the model changes?

Rerun the 25. Fix what broke. Date the file. Email v1.1 if you can. That is why you do not sell 1,000. Default: rerun the three proofs the week the model moves.

Can I copy a competitor and change "realtor" to "clinic"?

No. Copying someone else's stack and swapping the niche word is how you ship clever prompts that do not match the job. Write from the inside. Default: do not list a costume.

Is this the same as a skill pack?

No. Prompt stacks are paste-as-you-go. Skill packs are installed. Default: this path first; skill pack of the best five after a same-day use.

How long should each prompt be?

Long enough to name inputs, format, constraint, and done check. Usually a short paragraph. Default: one copy-paste block per prompt.

Should I offer a free 5-prompt teaser?

Skip the teaser in month one. Sell the 25. Default: no teaser.

What if the group bans links?

Help with two principles. Put the file in your profile. Do not fight the mods. Default: profile link, one comment, stop.

Do I need a brand name?

No. You need a niche word in the title. Default: searchable title, your name or no name.

Can I sell this as a subscription?

No. It is a $19 file. v1.1 is an email, not a monthly. Default: one-time $19.

What if nobody uses it the same day?

Ask. If they will not answer, prompt 1 or the SOP is weak. Fix prompt 1 this week. Default: fix prompt 1, do not add 75 more prompts.

Should I run ads to the listing?

Not until a stranger has bought from a title match or a personal share. Default: no ads in month one.
