What you are selling

A printable is a page someone will actually print, fill, and pin to a wall or drop in a binder. That is the whole product. Not a vibe. Not a mood board. A tool for a Tuesday problem: what to post this week, what to pack, what to check before a client walks in.

Search language is the product title. Weekly content tracker for solo hairstylists beats Cute planner 2026 because the first one names a person and a job. The second one is wallpaper. People searching Etsy or Google at 10pm are not shopping for cute. They are shopping for a page that stops the guessing.

Definition, in one breath

You pick one repeating job. You make one page that gets filled in. You print it at home at 100 percent, actual size. You photograph the filled page on a real table with the phone you already own. You list it at $7 to $12 with a title a tired person would type into a search bar. AI drafts the labels and the listing copy. You rewrite both in the language of the job. You do not generate faces, brands, or copyrighted characters. You do not list a bundle until someone has printed the single.

The file is cheap. The list is the real asset. Etsy is an aisle you rent. Use it if you have no traffic. Move them to email when you can.

The repeating job is the product

A repeating job is something the same person does every week, or every Saturday, or every client. Captions for a one-chair stylist. An opening checklist for a food-truck Saturday. Lesson notes for a tutor who runs four sessions after school. A van pack list for a mobile dog groomer. If the job is a one-off, you do not have a printable. You have a poster.

One page that gets filled in is the unit. Not a 40-page undated book. A grid a pen can hit, a title that names the job, a one-line instruction in the footer. Page two is a filled week, real texture, names blurred. Empty pretty is a hobby with a PDF export.

What this is not

This is not a 40-page undated planner with empty circles and a quote about blooming. Those exist by the thousand. They photograph well and convert poorly unless you already have a following that buys your taste.

This is not a wall print of someone else's illustration, a trademarked character, or a generated face. Your layout, your words, your simple shapes. If you cannot draw, use type, lines, and a two-color palette. Clean beats illustrated when the buyer is a working stylist, not a Pinterest board.

This is not a Canva template you leave editable so the buyer can make it theirs. An editable file is a different product, a different license, and a different support load. V1 is a locked PDF they print. If they want editable later, that is a $24 upgrade with a written license, not a free extra in the $9 zip.

Why this works now

Home printers did not go away. Salons, classrooms, kitchens, and vans still have a wall and a clip. The people who buy a $9 page are not waiting for an app. They want paper next to the chair, the stove, the crate of tools. Paper does not need a login. Paper does not vanish when a subscription lapses.

Search still works for a specific job. Booth renter content tracker is a query with a person behind it. Aesthetic planner 2026 is a query with a mood behind it. Mood shoppers bounce. Job shoppers print.

AI collapsed the copy cost. Labels and listing bullets used to take an afternoon. Now they take twenty minutes plus a rewrite. The rewrite is the work. A model does not know your printer. You do, after one test page.

What AI is for, and what it is not for

For: column labels in the language of the job. A first draft of the listing title and the five bullets. A one-line how-to in the footer. Alternate phrasings when Caption and Content pillar are both on the page and only one belongs.

Not for: a face, a child, a celebrity, a logo, a character, a lyric, a team mark. Not for in the style of. Not for a floral border you saw on a bestseller. Not for a 400-listing plan. Layout, print test, and a filled example are still human jobs. That is the gap you get paid for. Type and lines. If the page needs a drawing to work, the page is the wrong product.

Three anti-patterns

Anti-pattern one: the pretty empty grid. You spend six hours on a floral border and twenty minutes on the fields. The listing photo looks like a lifestyle magazine. The page, in a booth renter's hand, has nowhere to write the caption. Buyers leave a one-star that says cute but I still did not know what to post. You earned that star.

Anti-pattern two: the 400-listing sprint. You clone one Canva file into every pastel color and every vague niche without changing the job. Three related pages for one person beat four hundred cousins. Bundles come after a single prints, not as a way to look like a catalog.

Anti-pattern three: the borrowed picture. A cartoon character, a lyric, a league logo, an illustration in the style of a living artist. You will sell a few. Then the shop goes down. Type and lines are enough.

The deal you keep

You sell a $7 to $12 single. After someone has printed it, you sell a $19 bundle of three related pages for the same person. You keep the customer on an email list as soon as you can. You keep the how-to page on a site you own, even if Etsy is where the first twenty sales happen. You keep the right to update the file and send v1.1 to people who already paid.

You do not keep a fantasy of $10,000 months from one floral planner. You keep a small catalog you can name in one breath, a print-tested PDF, and a Tuesday problem you actually understand. That is the deal. It pays.

Who this is for — and who should skip it

This path fits if you can sit in Canva for two hours and ship a one-page tool that a stranger can fill without a video. You do not need to be a designer. You need margins, a hierarchy (title, then fields, then a one-line instruction), and the patience to print a test copy on the cheapest paper in the house.

It also fits if you already do the job on Tuesdays. A booth renter who already tracks captions on a sticky note is a better designer for this file than a person who has never stood behind a chair. Nearness to the job beats taste.

Fits if

You can name one person and one Tuesday problem in one line. You will print the page at 100 percent, actual size, and fill it with a pen. You will photograph the filled page on a real table. You will send ten messages to people who do the job. You will write a personal-use license in the footer and mean it. You can live with $9 as a first yes, wait to bundle until the single prints, leave faces and brands off the page, and ship v1.1 the same day a buyer writes.

Skip if

Skip generic aesthetic planners with no job. Skip trademarked characters. Skip 400 listings before one file prints. Skip this if you need rent this Friday — pair it with a paid week of work (path 7 or 12) and let printables compound. Skip this if you will not touch a printer. A page you have never printed is a screen decoration. One-stars start with clipped margins. Skip this if your only idea is a 2026 dated planner in five colors. That market is a landfill. Skip this if you want AI to draw the product. Labels and listing copy only. Skip this if you freeze at $9 and want to start at $27 with a 40-page book and no print test, or if you need the buyer on a call to explain a checkbox.

The honest middle

If you can design but do not know a job, shadow someone for a week or pick the job you already do. Watch what they write on a sticky note. That sticky note is the page. If you know the job but Canva scares you, use a simple table, 0.5 inch margins, two fonts, one color. Ugly and fillable beats pretty and empty. If you have three pages and zero listings, list the single, not the three. If you have 80 listings and no print test, archive the clones. Print the one you would use tonight.

Skills and time

Canva or Google Docs. A printer, home or library. A phone camera. A listing on Etsy or Stan. Ten DMs. A model window for labels and listing copy, then a rewrite. That is the stack.

Time: one evening for the page, one evening for the filled example and print test, one evening for the listing and ten asks. First sale can land the same week. If it does not, the title is wrong or you never showed the filled page. Budget: $0 if you already have Canva free or Docs, a way to print one test page, and a way to take $9.

Two-minute self-test

Answer these out loud. If you stall on two of them, this is not your first path this week.

  • Who is the person, in a job title, not a vibe?
  • What do they do every Tuesday that a page would stop them guessing?
  • Can you fill the page with a real week without inventing columns?
  • Will you print it tonight at 100 percent, actual size?
  • Will you photograph the filled page on a real table, pen in the shot?
  • Will you ask ten humans, not 400 listings?
  • Can you leave faces, brands, and copyrighted characters off the page?

Five or more yeses. Start. Four or fewer: pick a closer job or skip this path.

The buyer on the other side

A tired person who already tried a pretty planner and quit in week two. They have a wall, a clip, a booth, a van. They will pay $9 to stop guessing. They will judge you on whether the columns match the job, whether the checkbox takes a pen, and whether the print clipped. They will print page two, copy the pace, and fill page one next Tuesday. Design for them, not for a Pinterest board.

The offer, named in one sentence

The offer has four parts and none of them are a color palette.

Person: solo hairstylist, not creatives. Job: weekly content tracker, not planner. Format: one US Letter PDF, print-ready, with a filled example on page two. Price: $9 for the single. The $19 bundle of three related pages waits until the single has printed.

Fill this

A one-page [job] tracker for [person], print-ready, with a filled example, $9.

If you need and to name the person, you have two products. Split them. If you need and to name the job, you have two pages. Sell the first one. The second one is a sibling, later.

Write the sentence at the top of the Canva file. Put a shortened version in the listing title. The title is search language, not a brand name. Weekly Content Tracker for Solo Hairstylists — Printable PDF is a title a tired stylist would type. Glow Up Studio Planner is a name you liked at midnight.

Sentences that work

  • Weekly content tracker for one-chair hairstylists. Print it. Fill it at the chair. $9.
  • Opening-day checklist for a food-truck Saturday. One page. $9.
  • Lesson-note template for tutors who run four sessions after school. One page per student. $9.
  • Booth-renter tax envelope tracker. Twelve months on one page. $9.
  • Van pack list for mobile dog groomers. Print, laminate, wipe. $9.

Each sentence names a person and a repeating job. None of them name a palette. If your sentence needs a cartoon to make sense, you do not have an offer yet.

What they get

One US Letter PDF, print at 100 percent. A filled example so they are not staring at empty boxes. A one-line how-to in the footer. Personal use: print as many copies as they need for their own chair. Not a commercial license to resell your layout.

They get a version number in the footer so v1.1 can exist. They get an email you will answer. They get a refund sentence on the listing. They get a file named like a search, so they can find it in Downloads three Tuesdays from now.

What they do not get

An editable Canva link in v1. A commercial license. A dated 2026 planner. A matching Instagram theme. A community. A video course on how to use a checkbox. A bundle of three pages on day one. Faces, brands, or copyrighted characters. Lifetime updates you will not ship.

If they want editable, that is a later SKU with a written license and a higher price. If they want you to fill the week for them, that is a service, not a $9 PDF. If they want a 10-page undated book, they can buy someone else's landfill. You sell one page that gets filled in.

Packaging

File name: Content-Tracker-Solo-Hairstylist.pdf — not FinalFinal3.pdf. Cover of the listing is the filled page on a real table, photographed with a phone, pen in the shot. Not a mockup of a MacBook in a sunbeam. Version number in the footer so you can send v1.1. The listing title is the search. Five bullets. Personal-use line. Refund sentence. Print-at-100-percent instruction. Do not write a brand story. The page is a tool. Sell the tool.

One page, then a bundle

V1 is the single. You may sketch two sibling pages in the same week so you know they exist: a caption-starter sheet, a monthly overview, a packing list, a close-down sheet. You do not list them. You do not zip them. You do not discount the single to make a bundle look generous.

After someone has printed the single — a buyer note, a photo, a question about a column — you build the two siblings, print-test both, and list the $19 kit. Same person. Next obvious page. Same type, same margins. If nobody printed the single, you do not have a bundle problem. You have a title problem, or a photo problem, or a job that was a mood. Fix the single. Do not add pages to a page that does not print.

What done looks like

Done is someone prints the $9 file. Not someone likes the listing. Not someone saves it to a board. A print. Ink on paper. If you cannot imagine that, you built a mood board.

That is the only done that matters in week 1. A pretty mockup and zero prints is a hobby. A filled page on a real table, listed, asked about, and printed by someone who is not you, is a product. Harper will know which one she has by Sunday. So will you.

Definition of done

The single is done when a stranger can fill Tuesday without you talking, the PDF prints at 100 percent without clipping, and at least one person who is not you has put ink on the page. Everything else is decoration.

Done also means the title is search language, the listing photo is the filled page on a real table, and you have sent ten messages. The bundle is a later done.

The done bar for the single

  • Person and Tuesday problem written in one line.
  • Title in search language, not a cute brand name.
  • One-page tool with 0.5 inch safe margin.
  • Filled example on page two with a real week.
  • Print test at 100 percent, actual size, no clipping.
  • Checkboxes at least 0.25 inch. Fill-in lines near-black.
  • License: your layout, your words, no trademarked characters, no generated faces or brands.
  • Table photo of the printed, filled page, pen in the shot.
  • Test-buy from a second email, file opens, file prints.
  • Ten messages to people who do the job.
  • Version number and an email in the footer.

If three of those are missing, you have a draft. Keep going. Do not list a draft and improve it with one-stars.

Fairness test

Hand the printed page to someone who does the job. Do not explain it. If they can fill Tuesday without you talking, you shipped. If they ask where the caption goes, the columns are wrong. Fix the page, not the listing copy.

Would you sell this to a tired friend who does that job, at $9, without a speech? If you would apologize for the checkboxes or offer to walk them through, it is not fair yet. Fair means they can pin it next to the chair tonight. Fair means a refund in one sentence if the print clipped.

Technical done

PDF exports. Fonts outlined or standard. No Canva watermarks on the paid file. File name a tired person can find. Zip only later, for the bundle. Refund policy in one sentence on the listing. An email in the footer you will answer. Print instruction: 100 percent, actual size, not fit to page. Version number so v1.1 is a real file, not a guess.

Open the PDF on your phone. Open it on a desktop. Print a second copy after the export, not only the Canva print. Exports lie. Paper does not.

Not done yet

A Canva file you have not exported. A mockup with no print test. Forty pastel clones. A shop with a cute name and zero specific titles. A bundle listed before a single has printed. A generated illustration you could not defend to a lawyer. An editable link in a $9 zip. Those are hobbies with an Etsy password. A listing with sales and no print is not done either — ask if they printed it. If they did not, the photo lied or the columns did not match the job.

Pricing that matches a printed page

$7 to $12 for a single. $19 for three related pages. That is the window. $9 and $19 are home. Put the number on the listing. Do not hide it behind DM me.

The window

$7 is the floor if you are nervous and the page is one simple checklist. $9 is the default first printable: one page, a filled example, print-tested. $12 is fair when the how-to exists and you have ten sales. Stay in the window on the first file. This is not a $27 undated book. This is not a $3 race to the bottom.

The bundle is $19, and only after the single prints. Three related pages for the same person. Not five random pastels. Not a 10-page pack. Three. If you cannot name why the second and third pages belong next to the first, they do not belong in the zip.

Why not $27 on day one

You have no proof, no how-to, no reviews. A $9 page is an easy yes for a booth renter. A $27 undated book is a maybe they will not finish. Raise the single to $12 and the bundle to $24 when the how-to exists and you have ten sales. Do not start there.

$27 also trains you to overbuild. You will add quote pages and covers to justify the number. Then you have a planner. $9 keeps you honest. One page. One job. One print test.

Worked dollars

Harper lists a $9 tracker on Wednesday. Ten DMs. One public post of the filled page. Priya buys Friday and prints it at the salon. One more single on Saturday. $18 before fees. Not rent. Proof. The single printed.

Week 2 she adds the two siblings, lists the $19 bundle, and the next two buyers take the kit. Month one: 14 singles, 6 bundles = $240 before fees. A list of 20 people who printed something. That list is the asset. The $24 how-to on Stan in month two is how the asset pays a second time. $9 is the door. The bundle is the room next door, after someone has walked in.

What not to do with price

Do not price a one-page grid at $29 because you spent eight hours on flowers. Do not do $3 to race to the bottom, or $0 with a tip jar, or 14 upsells on the thank-you page. One single. After it prints, one bundle. A commercial license later, written, $49 or more, only if someone asks twice. Do not discount the single to $5 because week 2 was quiet. Quiet is usually the title, the photo, or the ten asks you did not send. Do not price by hours. Eight hours of floral work does not make a $29 product. It makes a $9 product with a worse margin.

Refunds

Refund on request. Keep the policy to one sentence. A fight over $9 costs more than $9. If they could not print, that is your export. Fix the file, refund, send v1.1 to everyone.

If they wanted a service, refund and clarify the listing: this is a file, not a social media manager. Do not invent a commercial SKU in the refund email.

When to raise

After ten sales and a how-to page: $12 single, $24 bundle. After a commercial request twice: add that SKU, written, $49 or more. Never raise by adding empty pages. Never raise because you got bored of $9. Email v1.1 free to people who already paid $9. Do not charge them again for a wider column.

The first 72 hours

Seventy-two hours is enough to list one page. It is not enough to build a shop. It is not enough to generate a catalog. One repeating job, one page that gets filled in, one print test, one table photo, ten asks. That is the whole window.

Hours 1-8: pick the job and sketch

Write the person and the Tuesday problem on a sticky note. One line. If it needs a slash, you have two people. Pick one. Sketch the columns on paper. If you cannot sketch it on a napkin, Canva will not save you.

Fill a sample week on the sketch with a real pen, from a real week you remember. If you have to invent columns to make the week fit, you are guessing the job. Shadow someone or pick a job you already do. Stop at hour 8 with a sticky note and a sketch you can fill. Do not open Canva until the sketch fills.

Hours 9-16: build the one page

Open Canva. US Letter. 0.5 inch margins. Title the job, not your brand. Fields a pen can hit. Checkboxes at least 0.25 inch. Black or near-black for fill-in lines. Light gray disappears on paper. Two fonts. One color besides black. Hierarchy: title, fields, one-line instruction in the footer.

Draft labels with AI if you want. Rewrite every label. Caption, not content pillar. Client first name, not persona. The model does not stand behind the chair. You do. Do not generate a border, a face, a logo, a character, or a floral. Type and lines.

Hours 17-24: fill, print, photograph

Fill page two with a real week. Invented data looks invented. Blur a name if you must. Keep the texture: the actual caption length, the actual yes/no on the photo, the actual Thursday that went sideways.

Print at 100 percent, actual size, not fit to page. Home printer or library. Fill it with the pen you actually own. If type hits the edge, fix the margin. If a checkbox is tiny, enlarge it. Print a second copy after the fix. This step is the product.

Photograph the filled page on a real table. Overhead, even light, pen in the shot. Phone camera. That photo is the listing image. Not a mockup generator. Not a MacBook in a sunbeam.

Hours 25-48: listing copy, license, export

Write the listing. Title in search language. First line that names the job. Five bullets. Personal-use line. Refund sentence. Print-at-100-percent instruction. Use AI for a first draft of the title and bullets if you want. Rewrite until it sounds like a person who does the job, not a listing template.

Footer of the PDF: personal use, print for your own chair, no reselling the PDF, your email, version number (v1.0, date). No trademarked characters anywhere. No generated faces. No brand marks.

Export PDF. Name the file like a search: Content-Tracker-Solo-Hairstylist.pdf. Open it on your phone. Print a copy of the export. If anything clips, fix the margin before you list. Confirm there is no Canva watermark on the paid file. You may sketch two sibling pages in a private file. You do not list them. The bundle waits.

Hours 49-72: test-buy, ten messages, one post

Test-buy from a second email. Etsy or Stan, whichever you listed on. File arrives. File opens. File prints. If the download fails, nothing else matters. Fix it before you send a single ask.

Then ten messages to people who do the job. Not a broadcast. I made a one-page tracker for [job] because I was tired of sticky notes. You do this every week. If it is useless, tell me. If it is useful, it is $9. [link]. One public post of the filled page, not the empty grid. Ask for a reply, not a follow.

Do not run Etsy ads. Do not clone the file into 40 colors. Do not list the bundle. If someone asks a question that means the columns are wrong, that fix is v1.1, and it belongs after a human has used the page.

What you do not do in 72 hours

You do not name a shop with a pun. You do not generate 12 pastel clones, buy a mockup pack, stretch Letter to A4, or prompt a cute mascot. One page. One listing. Ten asks. A print. That is a good 72 hours.

The path, step by step

Twelve steps. Stop at the one you have not done. Do not skip the print test. Do not skip the ten asks. Do not jump to the bundle.

Step 1. Name the person and the Tuesday problem

One line. Solo hairstylist who never knows what to post this week. If the line needs a slash, you have two people. Pick one. Write it on a sticky note. Put the sticky note at the top of the Canva file. Search language starts here: the person and the job will become the listing title.

Step 2. Sketch one page that gets filled in

Columns on paper. Idea, photo, caption, posted is a tracker. Pack, check, done is a list. If you cannot fill a sample week without inventing a column, you are guessing the job. The sticky note they already use is a better product than a Pinterest grid.

Step 3. Build the page in Canva

US Letter. 0.5 inch safe margin. Hierarchy: title, fields, one-line instruction. Two fonts, one color besides black. Checkboxes a pen can hit, at least 0.25 inch. Fill-in lines near-black. Draft labels with AI if you want. Rewrite every label in the language of the job. Do not generate faces, brands, characters, or a floral you saw on a bestseller. Type and lines.

Step 4. Fill page two with a real week

Blur a name if you must. Keep the texture. Empty grids do not sell. Filled grids sell. If you cannot fill a real week, you do not know the job yet. Do the job once this week, capture as you go, then fill the page. Invented data photographs like invented data.

Step 5. Print test at home at 100 percent

Actual size, not fit to page. Home printer or library. Fill it with a pen. If type hits the edge, fix the margin. If a checkbox is tiny, enlarge it. Print a second copy after the fix. Do not list before this.

Step 6. Photograph the filled page on a real table

Phone camera. Overhead, even light, pen in the frame. That photo is the listing. A lifestyle mockup is optional and later. Do not use a mockup generator as the only image. Buyers are shopping for a page they will put on a table. Show them a table.

Step 7. Write the listing title like a search

Weekly Content Tracker for Solo Hairstylists — Printable PDF. First line names the job. Five bullets. Personal-use line. Refund sentence. Print-at-100-percent instruction. AI can draft this. You rewrite it. If you delete every adjective (cute, aesthetic, glow), the title should still name a person and a job. If it does not, it is a mood board.

Step 8. License, export, test-buy

Footer: personal use, print for your own chair, no reselling the PDF, your email, version number. Your layout, your words. No trademarked characters, generated faces, or brands. Export PDF. Filename like a search. Test-buy from a second inbox. Open. Print. No Canva watermark. If the download fails, fix that before a single ask.

Step 9. List the $9 single

Etsy if nobody knows you. Stan or Stripe on a page you own, same file. Both, aisle first, if you have no traffic. Price $7 to $12, default $9. One listing. One photo of the filled page. Do not list the bundle. Do not list five colors. Do not run ads.

Step 10. Send ten messages and one public post

Ten people who do the job. Personal notes, not a blast. One public post of the filled page, not the empty grid. First sale is allowed to be someone you know. Ask if they printed it. Printed is the metric.

Step 11. Ship v1.1 after the first buyer note

If two people ask where a column is, or one person who used it says the posted column is too narrow, you move the column. Export. Bump the footer to v1.1, date. Email everyone who already paid. Do not take it personally. That note is the product improving. A one-star is what you get if you ignore it.

Step 12. Bundle only after a single prints

Someone printed the $9 file. Then two sibling pages for the same person. Same type, same margins, same print test, same filled examples. $19 for three related pages. Do not invent a new niche. After ten sales or 21 days, decide one change: title, columns, or the filled photo. Fix the one that prints, not a catalog that does not.

Worked example: Harper and the hairstylist tracker

Harper cuts hair two days a week and hates posting. She already fills a sticky note with this week's ideas: a before-and-after, a product she actually used, a Friday hours reminder. That sticky note is the product. She needs it to stop ripping.

Harper, the sticky note, the chair

The person is a one-chair stylist. The Tuesday problem is what to post this week. Harper copies the columns off her own note: idea, photo (yes/no), caption draft, posted (date), what happened. Five columns. One week. A title at the top. A one-line footer: Fill this on Monday. Pin it at the chair. Take the photo before you wash the color out.

She almost titled the file Glow Up Content Planner 2026. She wrote that on a scrap, looked at it, and crossed it out. Nobody at the chair searches for glow up. They search for what to post, hairstylist, weekly. Search language. She wrote Weekly Content Tracker for Solo Hairstylists on the next scrap and kept it.

What she shipped

A one-page weekly content tracker for one-chair hairstylists. Page two: her own week, filled, with a blur on a client first name. The Thursday caption was too long and she wrote too long in the what-happened column. That texture is why Priya believed it.

She did not ship the bundle on day one. She sketched a 12-caption-starter page in salon language and a monthly overview, then closed the file. The single had to print first.

She printed the tracker on the library printer for $0.20. Photographed it on the break table with a black pen. Listed on Etsy Wednesday night. Title: Weekly Content Tracker for Solo Hairstylists — Printable PDF. First line: Stop guessing what to post this week. One page. Print it. Fill it at the chair. Price: $9. No ads. No pastel clones.

The 72 hours

Wednesday 7pm: sticky note, napkin sketch, a real week filled on paper. Wednesday 9pm: Canva. Two fonts. Near-black lines. Labels drafted by a model, rewritten: Caption, not Content pillar. Thursday lunch: print test at the library. Checkbox too small. Enlarged. Printed again. Thursday night: filled page two, photo on the break table, listing, test-buy from her other email. The PDF opened. The export printed.

Friday: ten DMs to stylists she actually knows, plus one post in a booth-renter group she had helped in. The post was the filled page, not the empty grid. The caption was the first line of the listing, plus $9. No floral mockup. No I am so excited to share.

What happened, with dollars

Friday 4pm: a stylist named Priya buys the $9. Saturday morning Priya texts a photo of the page taped next to her mirror, two boxes already filled. That photo is the whole business. Someone printed it. It is a product, not a hobby.

Saturday: one more single from a woman in the same group. $18 before fees. Harper's first-week cash is small. Harper's first-week fact is large: ink on paper in a salon that is not hers.

She does not list the bundle on Saturday. She waits. Priya's photo is the green light, not a feeling.

What almost broke it

She almost used a floral Canva template that ate the margins. The library print saved her. The first test clipped the footer. She pulled the grid in, killed the flowers, printed again. She almost listed before printing, because the screen looked fine. The printer is the editor. She almost generated a cute scissors illustration in the style of a popular artist she follows. She deleted the prompt. Type and lines. She almost sent a broadcast to 80 people. She sent ten notes instead. Priya was number four.

v1.1 after Priya's note

Sunday night Priya emails: the posted column is too narrow for a date. Harper widens it, shortens the what-happened column by a hair, exports v1.1, emails both buyers. Subject: your tracker, slightly less annoying. That is quality. That is also how you do not get a one-star.

The listing photo stays the original break-table shot. The file behind the listing is v1.1. She does not remake the brand. She moves a column.

Monday she builds the two sibling pages she had sketched. Caption-starter sheet: 12 first lines in salon language. Monthly overview: four weeks, same columns, smaller. Print-tests both. Fills both with a real month. Lists the $19 bundle Tuesday of week 2. Title: Hairstylist Content Kit — Weekly Tracker + Captions + Monthly Overview. The next two buyers take the kit.

Ninety days, and the product-or-hobby test

41 sales. 19 of them bundles. A $24 how-to on her own Stan page that Etsy never sees. An email list of 28 people who printed something. Not a brand empire. A Tuesday product that prints. Harper still cuts hair. The files pay for the software and a Friday off.

The test she uses, and the test you should use this week: did someone print it? Priya printed it. Then 40 other people printed it. That is a product. A pretty mockup and zero prints would have been a hobby. Harper would have known by Sunday of week 1 either way. She listed one tracker. That is how you know.

Copy you can paste

Swap the job. Keep the constraints. Do not add hype. Fill the brackets. Send. The listing title is search language. The post is the filled page. The DM is one job, one price, one link.

Listing title

Weekly Content Tracker for Solo Hairstylists — Printable PDF

Other titles in the same shape:

Opening Day Checklist for Food Truck Saturdays — Printable PDF
Lesson Notes for After-School Tutors — One Page Printable
Van Pack List for Mobile Dog Groomers — Printable PDF

If you delete Printable PDF and the title still names a person and a job, you are close. If what remains is Studio Planner 2026, start over.

Listing first line and bullets

Stop guessing what to post this week. One page. Print it. Fill it at the chair. A filled example is on page two.

  • One US Letter PDF, print at home at 100 percent, actual size
  • Built for one-chair stylists, not agencies
  • Columns for idea, photo, caption, posted
  • Includes a filled example so you are not staring at empty boxes
  • Personal use. Print as many copies as you need for your own chair

Bundle title (only after the single prints)

Hairstylist Content Kit — Weekly Tracker + Captions + Monthly Overview

First line for the bundle: Three pages for the same chair. The weekly tracker you may already have, plus a caption-starter sheet and a monthly overview. $19.

Post (filled page, not a mood)

I printed the page I actually use at the chair. One week of posts, no guessing. $9. Link in comments. If you want the empty floral version, this is not that.

DM to ten people who do the job

I made a one-page tracker for [job] because I was tired of sticky notes. You do this every week. If it is useless, tell me. If it is useful, it is $9. [link]

Checkout blurb

$9 for the tracker. Personal use. Refund if you ask. Print at 100 percent, actual size. Page two is a filled week so you can see the pace.

Note after purchase

Your file: [link]. Print at 100 percent, actual size. Page two is a filled week so you can see the pace. If a column is wrong for your chair, reply. I update these.

Follow-up, same thread: Did you print it? If a column fought you, tell me which one. I will fix the file for everyone. That question is how v1.1 happens.

Refund reply

Done. Refunded. If the print clipped, that is on me — tell me the printer and I will fix the margin for everyone.

Replies: editable, or a team license

V1 is a locked PDF you print. Editable Canva is a different file, a different license, and a different price. I do not include it in the $9 zip. If two people ask, I will list it as a $24 upgrade. Until then, print it.

Personal use: your chair, your copies. Not a license to resell the PDF or to hand it to a staff of twelve as your product. If you need commercial rights, that is a separate SKU with a written sentence, and it is not $9. If that SKU does not exist yet, it does not exist. I will refund you if you bought thinking it did.

What you do not write

Cute planner magic. Boss babe. Unlimited commercial license in a $9 file. A promise it will grow your Instagram. Generated-art language. In the style of. A brand story. A countdown. The page is a tool. Sell the tool.

Week-by-week if you have a job

Assume evenings. This is four weeks to a printed page and, if it earns it, a bundle. No 400-listing sprint. No ads in week 1. No public launch party.

Week 1, day by day

Monday: person, problem, napkin sketch. Fill a sample week on paper. Do not open Canva if the sketch will not fill.

Tuesday: one page in Canva. Labels rewritten. No generated art. Stop at a page you would pin next to your own chair.

Wednesday: filled example, print test at 100 percent, photo on a real table. If it clips, fix and print again. Listing title in search language. Export. Test-buy from a second email.

Thursday and Friday: ten DMs and one public post of the filled page. First sale is allowed to be someone you know. Ask if they printed it.

Saturday and Sunday: answer humans. Do not clone colors. Do not list a bundle. Do not run ads. If someone printed it, you have a product. If nobody printed it, you have a hobby with a listing. Either way, you will know.

Week 2: v1.1 and, only if it printed, the bundle

Answer every question like a person. If two people trip on the same column, or one person who used it sends a note, ship v1.1. Email everyone who paid. Count prints and questions, not listing views.

If someone printed the single, build the two sibling pages. Same person. Next job. Print-test both. Filled examples. List the $19 bundle. One more share in the same room.

If nobody printed it, do not build the bundle. Change the title to search language. Replace the listing image with the filled page if you used a mockup. Send ten new asks. The job in the title is usually the problem, not the prose.

Start the how-to draft this week either way. A few paragraphs on the same job, on a page you own. This is how Etsy buyers become a list.

Week 3: teach the page, do not add a catalog

One post or email that teaches one column. Soft link. Example: the what-happened column is where you write too long, not where you perform. If you are not public, send three more personal messages instead of posts.

Invite Etsy buyers off the aisle with a next page is on my list line inside the PDF, if you have sales. If you have no sales, still do not add 40 listings. One job. One title. Ten more asks.

Week 4: decide, do not sprawl

Decide: same person, next Tuesday problem, or stop. A second job is allowed after the first has a how-to and a handful of sales. Same grid, new language, new filled week, new print test. Default: week 4, not day 2. If nothing moved in 21 days of honest asks, quit the title, not by opening a second shop.

After

A small catalog you can name in one breath. Monthly v1.x if a column dates. That is maintenance. The path is not a 400-listing factory. The how-to page, the list, and the next related page for the same person are the compounding. Pretty clones are not.

The quality bar

Quality is a page a tired person can fill at the chair without you in the room, printed at 100 percent, no clip, no tiny checkbox, no light-gray line that vanished. Taste is optional. Fillable is not.

Specs that keep you out of one-star land

  • Black (or near-black) for all fill-in lines. Light gray disappears on paper.
  • Checkboxes at least 0.25 inch. Pens are thicker than cursors.
  • 0.5 inch safe margin. Printers eat edges.
  • Print at 100 percent, actual size, in the listing instructions.
  • Fonts large enough to read at arm's length on a wall.
  • No watermarks on the file they paid for. Previews may be marked. The product may not.
  • Version number and an email in the footer.
  • Filename a tired person can find.

If you skip the print test, you are guessing every one of these. Paper is the review you give yourself.

The filled page is the quality

Empty pretty is below-bar. Filled, printed, photographed on a real table is above-bar. If you would not pin your own page next to the chair, do not list it.

Page two is not a decoration. It is the instruction manual. A stranger copies the pace. If page two is fake-clean — every caption perfect, every box ticked — it reads as a mood board. Keep one Thursday that went sideways.

What you do not generate

No faces. No children. No celebrities. No brand marks. No league logos. No cartoon characters. No lyrics. No in the style of a living artist. No recreation of a bestseller's floral. AI is for labels and listing copy, rewritten. The shop's name is attached to the file. Type and lines do not get you a takedown. A generated princess in a salon does.

If the page needs a drawing to work, the page is the wrong product. Pick a different Tuesday problem.

Canva Pro photos are not yours to sell unless the license says they are. When unsure, do not. Your type is enough.

Test 1: the napkin test

Columns make sense on paper before Canva. If you cannot fill a week on a napkin, you cannot fill it in a PDF.

Test 2: the print test

100 percent, actual size, home or library. No clip. Checkbox takes a pen. Lines are visible. Do this on the export, not only inside Canva.

Test 3: the stranger test

Someone who does the job fills it without you talking. If they ask where the caption goes, the columns are wrong. Fix the page.

Test 4: the table-photo test

The listing image is the filled page on a real table, pen in the shot, taken with a phone. If the only image is a mockup, you are not ready.

Test 5: the quiet-title test

Delete every adjective (cute, aesthetic, glow, magic, undated). The title should still name a person and a job. If it does not, it is a mood board.

License

Your layout, your words, no trademarked characters, no generated faces or brands, no Canva Pro photos you do not have the right to sell. Personal use in the footer. Commercial only as a separate SKU with a written sentence, $49 or more, only after someone asks twice. Editable Canva is a later SKU, not a free extra in the $9 zip.

What to measure

Vanity is listing views. Money is conversion and refunds. The only week-1 metric that tells you the truth is a print. Someone put ink on the page, or they did not. Hearts on Etsy cannot tell you that.

Count these

  • Print tests you did yourself (yes/no, 100 percent, actual size).
  • Listing live, title in search language, photo of the filled page on a table.
  • Ten asks sent.
  • Sales of the $9 single.
  • Prints: ask Did you print it? A sale that never prints is a soft no.
  • Questions that mean the columns are wrong.
  • v1.1 shipped (yes/no).
  • Bundle listed only after a print (yes/no).
  • Refunds, with a one-word reason (clipped, wanted-editable, wanted-a-service, never-opened).

Week 1

Listings live: one. Print tests done. Ten asks sent. Sales. Questions. Prints. If you have a pretty mockup and zero prints, you have a hobby. Write that down. Do not soothe it with a second listing.

Day 30

Conversion rate on the listing (a few percent is real). Refunds (over 10 percent means the photo lied or the print clipped). Emails captured. Bundle attach rate, if the bundle exists (if nobody takes the $19, the siblings are not related). v1.1 sent. How-to draft started.

A healthy day-30: one job, one single that has printed, a v1.1 if anyone tripped, a bundle only if the single printed, 0 to 1 refunds you already fixed. A shop with 80 listings and $40 is the anti-pattern. Keep the three that print.

Day 90

A catalog you can name in one breath. A how-to that ranks or an email list. Repeat buyers. Cash in the $7 to $12 and $19 window, totaled. If you have 400 listings and $40, you ran the anti-pattern. If you have $0, the failure is usually title, unsent asks, or a photo of an empty grid. It is rarely the market.

Ignore these

Hearts on Etsy. Pinterest impressions. Follower count. Time in Canva. How many fonts you tried. How many pastel clones you could make. Mockup-generator output. A shop that looks busy. Pending Etsy ads.

Spreadsheet

One line a week is enough:

date | title | source | $9 or $19 | printed (y/n) | refund | question | email captured | version

If the printed column is always empty, you are not asking. Ask. If the question column repeats the same column name, that is v1.1, this week, not a new listing.

Objections you will hear

You will hear these from yourself first. Then from a friend who sells 400 listings. Then from a buyer who wanted a different product. Answer them once, in this file, so you do not argue them in a comment.

Etsy is too saturated

Shops with huge catalogs still win on the specific titles, not the pile. Weekly content tracker for solo hairstylists is not competing with cute planner 2026. It is competing with a sticky note. Saturation is what people say when they do not want to pick a job.

I cannot draw

Good. Type, lines, two colors. The job is the art. A drawing you generated is a liability. A checkbox a pen can hit is a product.

I need 400 listings to get traffic

You need one title a human would search and ten asks. 400 listings is how you hide a bad page. Traffic to a mood board is still a hobby. One print is a business.

People want editable Canva

Some do. That is a later SKU with a license. V1 is a locked PDF they print. Editable is support, versioning, and people breaking your grid. Charge more, later. Do not include it in the $9 zip because you are afraid of a no.

AI should generate the art

Not for a file you sell. Labels and listing copy, rewritten. Not stolen styles. Not a character. Not a face. Not a brand. Your shop's name is attached. If the page needs a drawing to work, pick a different page.

$9 is too cheap to bother

$9 is a yes. The bundle and the list are the business. A $47 empty planner is a no. You are not too good for a printed page. You are too early for a $27 book.

I will run ads on day one

Not in week 1. Ten asks and a specific title first. Ads on a generic planner light money on fire. Ads on a title nobody would search do the same. Prove a print organically. Then, maybe, a small ad on that exact title.

US Letter is wrong for my country

Sell the size your person prints. Default: one size you have printed, then the other when a buyer asks twice. Do not stretch Letter to A4. Rebuild the margin. A stretched grid is a one-star about clipping, written in a different paper size.

Nobody will pay for a PDF they could make in Canva

They could. They will not, on a Tuesday at 10pm, when they need the columns to already exist. They are paying to skip the guessing. If they already have a page they like, they should not buy.

I should wait until I have a shop name and a brand kit

You should wait until the page prints. A shop name is not a product. Harper listed under her own name and a search title. The brand kit can wait until someone who is not you has ink on the page.

What this path feeds next

Printables are a front door, not a dead end. Cheap files make a list. The list buys a playbook (path 1), a skill pack (path 2), a live drop (path 17), or a how-to you host. Do not open every door this month. Get a print first.

Upstream: what you need before this

You need a job you understand. You do not need a following. You do not need a playbook first, but a playbook makes the how-to easy. You need a printer, a phone, and ten names. If you have never done the job, do not invent the columns. Shadow, or pick the job you already do, or skip this path for a service week and come back with scars.

Downstream: the same person, the next product

  • How-to page / newsletter (path 5) for the same person. The next page is on my list line inside the PDF is the move off Etsy.
  • Templates and SOPs (path 6) if they want the digital version of the same job: a Notion or Sheet that does what the paper did.
  • Productized service (path 7) when they ask you to fill the week for them. That is a different number. Do not hide it inside $9.
  • Membership (path 14) only after they already print your pages and come back. A membership for people who never printed the $9 file is a chat you will resent.

The how-to is the real second product

After the single prints, write the how-to on a site you own. How I fill the Monday page at the chair. Four hundred words. One photo of the filled page. A link to the $9 file and, if it exists, the $19 bundle. Etsy does not own that page. The list that page builds is the asset the aisle cannot take.

Harper's $24 how-to on Stan is this. Etsy never saw it. The 28 people who printed something did.

Services that grow out of a page that prints

If two buyers ask you to fill the week, you have a productized service: a Monday caption pack, delivered as a filled page. Price it as work, not as a file. Custom layout is a small project, quoted, not a $5 tweak. Do not take custom in week 1.

Never

A replica of someone else's planner catalog. A shop of trademarked characters. A funnel that withholds the PDF until they sit through a webinar. A second niche on day 2. Generated art so the listing looks like a brand. The next path is the one the people who printed the page asked for.

Mistakes that kill this path

These are not personality flaws. They are skips. Each one has a recovery you can do this week.

1. Generic aesthetic planners with no job

Recovery this week: rename to a person plus a Tuesday. Rebuild columns from a sticky note a real human uses. Kill the quote about blooming.

2. Trademarked characters, generated faces, borrowed brands

Recovery this week: delete the listing today. Keep type and lines. If you already sold a few, refund, take it down, do not argue with the platform. The shop's name is attached.

3. 400 listings before one file prints

Recovery this week: archive the clones. Print-test the one you would use. List that one. Send ten asks. Do not unarchive anything until that one prints.

4. Listing photo of an empty pretty grid

Recovery this week: fill it, print it, photograph it on a real table tonight, pen in the shot. Replace the listing image before you send another ask.

5. Light gray lines and tiny checkboxes

Recovery this week: black lines. Checkboxes at least 0.25 inch. Re-export. Print. Email v1.1 to anyone who already paid.

6. Fit to page in the instructions

Recovery this week: write 100 percent, actual size. If they already clipped, refund, fix the margin, send the new file.

7. Bundling before a single prints

Recovery this week: unlist the bundle. Leave the $9 single. Ask the buyers if they printed it. Build siblings only after a yes.

8. Editable link in a $9 zip

Recovery this week: lock v1. Remove the Canva link. Sell editable later, written license, higher price. Email the people who got the link and tell them personal use still holds.

9. Canva Pro photos, watermarks, ads on day one, or FinalFinal3.pdf

Recovery this week: remove photos you cannot sell. Confirm the export has no watermark. Pause the ads. Ten asks. Specific title. Rename the file like a search. Test-buy so the new name is what they download. Your type is enough.

10. Skipping the print test, or ignoring the first buyer note

Recovery this week: library printer, tonight. 100 percent, actual size. Fix what clips. Add an email and a version number to the footer. Answer the note. Ship v1.1. The screen always looks fine. A one-star is what you get if the posted column stays too narrow and you never hear it.

Someone prints the $9 file. That is the path. A pretty mockup and zero prints is a hobby. Fix toward a print. Do not fix toward a catalog.

Tools — only what you need

Canva, a home or library printer, a phone for the mockup, Stan or Etsy, AI for labels and listing copy — not for stolen art. That is the stack. Everything else is delay.

Design

Canva free is enough. US Letter. 0.5 inch margins. Two fonts. One color besides black. Google Docs with a table is the $0 path. InDesign is not required. You are making a page a pen can hit, not a brand system.

Export PDF. Open it on a phone. Print the export. If the font is tiny or the checkbox collapsed, fix the file, export again.

Print

Any printer. Library is allowed. 100 percent, actual size. One test page is cheaper than one one-star. Print the sketch, print the Canva draft, print the export. Paper is the editor. If you do not have a printer at home, the library is the tool.

Selling

Etsy for the aisle. Stan or Stripe Payment Link for a page you own. Both, aisle first, if nobody knows you. After the first twenty sales, invite them off Etsy with a next page is on my list line inside the PDF. Do not wait for a full site. A Stan page whose title matches the listing is enough.

AI, used narrowly

One model window you already use. Labels. Listing title. Five bullets. Footer how-to. Alternate column names. Then you rewrite. You do not generate faces, brands, copyrighted characters, or florals in the style of anyone. You do not ask it for a 400-listing plan. You do not ship the first draft of the listing.

Delivery and the second email

The platform's download. Test from a second email. Do not gate the PDF behind a webinar. Create the second email before you list. Buy your own product. If the download never arrives, fix that before you send a single ask.

Do not add yet

A mockup generator subscription. A trademark lawyer for a cute name. A 400-listing uploader. Ads. A course on Etsy SEO. Pinterest management software. Canva Pro so you can delay the print test. A mascot. An A4 version you have not rebuilt. An editable SKU. A commercial SKU. Those wait until a stranger has printed the $9 file.

The $0 path

Google Docs table. 0.5 inch margins. Library print. Phone photo on a real table. Stripe Payment Link or Stan if you already have it. Ten DMs. A free-tier model for labels, rewritten. That can produce the first $9 without Etsy. You do not need a new laptop.

Setup order

Sticky note. Napkin sketch, filled. Canva or Docs, one page. Labels rewritten. Filled page two. Print test. Table photo. Listing title in search language. Footer license and version. Export. Filename like a search. Checkout. Test-buy from a second email. Ten asks. v1.1 after a human note. Bundle only after a print. Do not reorder this to put the shop name first.

Checklist

Print this. Tick it with a pen. If a line is unchecked, that is the next evening. Do not list a draft.

Before you open Canva

  • Person and Tuesday problem written in one line
  • Napkin sketch of one page that gets filled in
  • A sample week filled on the sketch without inventing columns
  • You would pin this next to your own chair
  • No faces, brands, or copyrighted characters in the plan

Before you list

  • One-page tool in Canva (or a Docs table) with 0.5 inch safe margin
  • Title in search language, not a cute brand name
  • Labels rewritten in the language of the job
  • Filled example on page two with a real week
  • Print test at 100 percent, actual size, no clipping
  • Checkboxes at least 0.25 inch
  • Fill-in lines near-black, not light gray
  • Table photo of the printed, filled page, pen in the shot
  • License: your layout, your words, no trademarked characters
  • File named like a search, not FinalFinal3.pdf
  • Version number and an email in the footer
  • No Canva watermark on the paid file
  • No generated art, no Canva Pro photos you cannot sell

Before you send ten asks

  • Test-buy from a second email, file opens, file prints
  • Listing first line names the job
  • Five bullets, personal-use line, refund sentence
  • Print at 100 percent, actual size, in the instructions
  • Price $7 to $12, default $9, on the page
  • Ten names written down
  • Bundle is not listed yet

After the first sale

  • Ask: did you print it? Which column fought you?
  • v1.1 if a column is wrong, emailed to everyone who paid
  • How-to page started, even as a draft, aimed at the same job
  • Bundle of two sibling pages only after a single prints
  • Spreadsheet: date, title, $9 or $19, printed, refund, question
  • You still would pin this page next to your own chair

Stop-doing

  • No ads until a specific title converts
  • No 400 pastel clones
  • Commercial license is a separate SKU or does not exist yet
  • A4 only after someone asks twice, rebuilt, not stretched
  • Do not list the bundle because week 2 felt quiet

FAQ

Do I start on Etsy or on my own site?

If nobody knows you, Etsy is the aisle. List the $9 single, and put the same file on a Stan or Stripe page. After the first twenty sales, invite them off Etsy with a next page is on my list line inside the PDF. Default: both, aisle first. Do not wait for a full site to list the page.

US Letter or A4?

Sell the size your person prints. US-heavy jobs: Letter first, A4 as a second file if you can keep the grid honest. Do not stretch Letter to A4. Rebuild the margin. Default: one size you have printed, then the other when a buyer asks twice.

Can I sell a fillable PDF they type in?

Yes, later. V1 is print. Fillable fields break on half the phones people open Etsy on. If you add fillable, keep a print version in the zip. Default: print only until someone asks twice.

How many listings before I quit?

One job, one single, ten asks, one how-to draft. Give that 21 days. If nothing moved, the job in the title is wrong or you never showed the filled page. Quit the title, not by opening listing forty. Default: do not add the bundle until the single prints.

What about commercial licenses for other sellers?

A separate SKU, written, $49 or more, only after someone asks twice. Do not bundle commercial rights into $9. Default: personal use only.

Is a wall print a printable in this path?

If they will pin it and use it, yes. If it is a quote about blooming, no. Default: a tool they fill, then a wall version of the same job if it earns it.

Should I watermark the preview?

The listing image is the filled page on a real table. You may mark a preview PDF. Never mark the file they paid for. Default: photo of the print, unpaid file clean.

What do I do when a buyer wants a custom version?

Quote a custom as a small project (path 20 or 7), not as a $5 tweak. Default: no custom in week 1. A second SKU if two people ask for the same change. v1.1 is a fix for everyone, not a custom for one.

Can I use Canva Pro photos, or AI images, in a file I sell?

Read Canva's license. When unsure, do not. Type and lines do not get you a takedown. Do not generate faces, brands, or copyrighted characters. Do not prompt in the style of a living artist. Default: no stock photos and no generated art in v1.

How do I handle refunds?

Refund if they ask. Fix the file if the print clipped. One sentence on the listing. Default: refund, then v1.1 to everyone. A fight over $9 costs more than $9.

Should I run Etsy ads?

Not in week 1. Ten asks and a specific title first. Default: organic plus DMs until you have a conversion and a print. Ads on a generic planner light money on fire.

When do I add a second person, or a bundle?

Bundle: after the first single has printed, two sibling pages for the same person, $19. Second person: after the first job has a how-to and a handful of sales, or after 21 days of honest asks. Same grid, new language, new filled week, new print test. Default: week 4 for a second person. No bundle on day 1.

Can I sell the same file on Etsy and on my site?

Yes. Same PDF. Different customers. Keep the version number in the footer so you update both. Default: both, aisle first.

How do I price a 10-page pack?

Do not, on day one. Three related pages at $19 is the pack, and only after the single prints. A 10-page undated book slides you back into generic planner land. Default: one page, one job, then three pages for the same job.

What if I hate Canva?

Google Docs, a table, 0.5 inch margins, export PDF. Ugly and fillable beats pretty and empty. Default: the tool you will actually open tonight.

How do I know if this is a product or a hobby?

Someone printed it, or they did not. A pretty mockup and zero prints is a hobby. A filled page on a real table, listed, asked about, and printed by someone who is not you, is a product. List one tracker this week. You will know by Sunday. Default: believe the print, not the mockup.

PATH 10

Creator ads with AI scripts

Brands need simple product videos. You do not need to be famous. You need to be clear.

You are comfortable on camera. You can hold a product and talk.
First sale
One paid brief for two videos.
Time to first
7–21 days
Cash window
$150–$800 for a first two-video pack
Tools
Phone, CapCut, a rate card, AI for script outlines only.
Leave this alone
Working for exposure. Promising virality.
