What a live drop actually is

The definition

A live drop is a date, a file, and a checkout. You announce a time. You go live for about twenty minutes. You show the pack on screen. People buy while you are still talking. That is the whole machine.

It is not a webinar. It is not a masterclass. It is not an hour of origin story before a slide that says "link in bio." You are not teaching a course. You are holding up a finished thing and letting people take it.

What this is not

It is not a talk show. It is not an accountability theater for a pack you have not exported. It is not a fake "only three left" on a PDF you can copy forever. It is not dual-streaming four platforms while you fumble one URL. It is not going live every day until the algorithm likes you.

It is not a $197 workshop with worksheets and a bonus coaching call. If you want high-ticket, that is a different path. This path is a $19–$47 file plus a twenty-minute show.

Why live still converts a file

A $29 pack on a quiet page asks the buyer to trust a stranger and a screenshot. A live drop lets them watch you open the file, click around, and answer one question out loud. Trust happens in public. That is why a plain pack can outsell a prettier one on a dead landing page — the live is the proof.

AI packs are easy to fake in a carousel. They are hard to fake with a screen share. You open page one. You run one example. You show the edit. That is more proof than a designed ad.

Live also forces a date. Dates make tired people decide. A quiet page waits forever. A Thursday at 7 does not.

What scarcity is allowed to mean

Scarcity is a date, a cohort, or a version. "I walk through this file Thursday at 7. After that you can still buy the pack on the page, but you miss the walkthrough." That is honest. "Only three left" on a digital file you can copy forever is a lie. People who buy from you once will remember the lie.

A version is also real. "This is the April pack. The next rewrite ships in six weeks." A cohort is real. "Twelve people get the live Q&A with this purchase. After twelve, the file is still for sale, the room is closed." Pick one form of scarcity. Write it down. Keep it.

If the pack is not finished, you do not have a drop. You have a promise, and promises do not check out.

Three anti-patterns

Anti-pattern one: fake stock. Countdown stickers, "2 spots," a price that "dies at midnight" when you will sell the same file on Saturday. Recovery this week: delete the sticker. Write the real date. Keep the price.

Anti-pattern two: going live with a draft. You promise a zip you have not exported. Checkout fails. Recovery this week: export, phone-check, test-buy from a second email. Then announce.

Anti-pattern three: daily lives. You train people to ignore you. Recovery this week: one dated Thursday. Next drop when you have a new version, a new sample, or a new audience. Not tomorrow.

The deal you keep

You keep a time, a finished file, and an honest scarcity line. They get a demo they can see and a checkout that delivers tonight. You will not invent a shortage. They will not get a course they did not buy.

The live is the event. The page is the store. Both exist the same night.

Who this is for — and who should skip it

Fits if

This path fits if you already have a finished pack from an earlier path: a playbook, a skill pack, a prompt stack, a template bundle. You can talk for twenty minutes without freezing. You have one platform where at least a few dozen people already watch or follow you. You do not need a huge audience. You need a time, a file, and the nerve to press Go Live.

It fits if you can demo the product with your screen, not just describe it. It fits if you can keep a Thursday. If you cancel lives, this path will embarrass you.

It fits if you have sold the file quietly, or you could, and you want a burst instead of a drip. If you need cash this week and the file is ready, this is one of the fastest paths in the suite.

Skip if

Skip it if the pack is not done. Skip it if you cannot be on a screen share without your voice leaving. Skip it if you only have a fake countdown and no real date. Skip it if you have never tested the checkout from a second email.

Skip it if both TikTok and Instagram are empty and you have no private list. This is not your first path. Finish path 1, 2, 3, or 6. Get a small audience on one platform. Then drop.

Skip it if you will discount live because the room is small. Holding the number is the job.

Skip it if you need a webinar funnel, a wait-room video, and an on-air producer to feel ready. Those are for people who already sell out rooms. You are dating a Thursday.

The honest middle

You have a $29 PDF that sold two copies from a quiet page, forty people who watch your Stories, and a Thursday night you will not cancel. That is enough. Sage's first useful room was eleven. Yours can be smaller.

If you have a pack and no audience, sell quiet first. Two stranger sales prove delivery. Then drop.

Skills and time

Skills: finish a file, keep a clock, share a screen, say a URL slowly, end on purpose. You do not need a personality brand. You can be a voice and a cursor.

Time: one evening to freeze the product and write the two-minute card. One day of two announcements and five DMs. Twenty minutes live. Thirty minutes after for the store page and notes. Then you stop.

Two-minute self-test

Answer yes or no.

  1. Is the pack exported, named like a human, and openable on a phone?
  2. Have you test-bought the checkout from a second email and received the file?
  3. Can you name a day and hour in the next seven days you will not cancel?
  4. Can you demo the first three pages without hunting eight folders?
  5. Will you hold the price if only three people show up?

If 1 or 2 is no, finish the pack and the pipe. If 3, 4, or 5 is no, pick a quiet page this week, not a live. A cancelled live costs more trust than a quiet week.

The offer, named in one sentence

Fill-in-the-blank

Write this before you pick a thumbnail: "Thursday 7pm I show the [named pack]. Twenty minutes. Link in bio. $[price]. After the live the walkthrough is gone; the file stays on the page."

That sentence is the offer. Everything else is decoration. If you cannot say it in one breath, you are stacking too many bonuses.

Five sentences that work

  • Thursday 7pm Eastern. I walk through the realtor listing pack on my screen. Twenty minutes. $29. After that the walkthrough is over; the pack stays on the page.
  • Saturday 10am. I open the bookkeeper follow-up stack, run one inbox example, and leave. $19. Link in bio the whole time.
  • Wednesday 8pm. Skill pack for solo dentists: ten posts, three examples, one-page install. $39. Twelve people get the live Q&A; then the room closes, file stays.
  • Friday noon. April version of the listing pack. I show what changed. $47. Next rewrite is six weeks out.
  • Tonight 7. Template bundle for Google Business posts. Twenty minutes, $29, instant download. Miss the live, still buy the zip.

What sits in the sentence

  • A day and a clock time in the buyer's timezone, or a timezone named out loud.
  • A file with a job in the title, not "my AI pack."
  • A price they can hear once and remember: $19, $29, $39, or $47.
  • A reason to show up live that is not fake stock.

What they get

The pack. Instant download. A twenty-minute walkthrough if they show up. Answers about the file, not about your life story. A store page afterward if they miss it.

What they do not get

A 40-minute bonus training. A private podcast. "I'll also critique your account." A membership. An automation setup. A surprise course at minute sixteen. A discount because they asked in the comments.

Packaging

The drop is the pack plus the twenty-minute show. If you want a higher ticket, that is a different path. Keep this one boring and buyable.

Checkout title matches the pack. Price is visible. File delivers. Bio link is live at least 24 hours before. Short URL on paper so you can say it.

Pick one scarcity: date, cohort, or version. Write it on the card. Do not mix all three in one breath.

What done looks like

Definition

Done is a live that produces at least one checkout from someone who is not you. The replay or the static page is up within two hours of ending. The link still works the next morning. You wrote down what people asked, what they bought, and what confused them.

If zero people bought, it is still a finished live if you showed the product and the link worked. You do not declare the path dead after one quiet Thursday. You also do not go live again tomorrow to chase the feeling.

Fairness test

Could a tired person who joins at minute four still tell what the file is, what it costs, and where to buy it? If not, you lectured. If yes, you dropped.

Would a buyer who paid during the live have the file before they went to bed? If delivery waits until morning, you are not done. Fix the pipe before you sleep.

Is the scarcity line still true the next morning? If you said the walkthrough was tonight-only and then you stay live until 8:15 because a friend was driving home, you taught them your dates are decoration.

Technical done

  • File exported. Filename human. Opens on a phone.
  • Checkout test-bought from a second email. File arrived.
  • Bio link live. Short URL on paper.
  • First two minutes on a card, rehearsed twice out loud.
  • Day, clock, timezone on a calendar you will keep.
  • Second device on the order screen.
  • Static page or pinned post template ready to publish the same night.

Not-done-yet list

  • A talking-head intro sequence. Not done-yet. Test the checkout.
  • Dual-stream, wait-room, webinar platform. Not done-yet.
  • Fake timer, "ONLY 2 SPOTS," a price drop in minute eighteen. Never done.
  • A second product added because the room went quiet. Not done. One file.
  • Replay as a requirement. Nice if you have it. The static page is required.
  • Going live with a folder of notes. Not a drop. A promise.

The live itself, done: you started within two minutes of the announced time. You showed the file in the first three minutes. You said the price and the URL out loud at least four times. Twenty minutes, maybe twenty-five if questions are real. Then you leave.

Pricing

Ranges

The cash window is a burst of the $19–$47 file. Live does not magically make a $197 pack feel cheap. Live makes a small file feel urgent and clear.

The numbers that hold up:

  • $19 if the pack is thin and this is your first public drop.
  • $29 if it is a complete job: prompts plus examples plus a one-page how-to. This is the default. Sage sells here.
  • $39 if you include a filled sample the buyer can copy.
  • $47 if the pack already sold quietly and you are using the live as a version event, not a rescue.

Worked dollars: Sage, $29, one Wednesday pre-sale, four during the live, one overnight. Six packs in two days. $174. Room of eleven. That is a real first drop, not a stadium.

When to raise

Raise when you introduce a version that actually added examples, not because you turned a camera on. If the pack already sells at $19 on the page, keep $19 or ship a $29 version with a filled sample. Do not raise only for the live.

After three drops, if live checkouts are real and the page also sells, you may sit at $39. Do not leap to $97 because a comment asked for a course.

Refunds in one sentence

If the file does not arrive or you showed a different product than they paid for, refund the same night; if they bought the right file and just changed their mind, refund on request inside 7 days and do not haggle on live.

Never-charge

You never run a fake "only 3 left at this price." You never drop the price in minute eighteen because the room is small. You never add a $9 upsell on the fly. You never charge a "live ticket" for a digital file you will sell on the page tomorrow at the same price unless the ticket is clearly the walkthrough and the file is separate — and even then, this path stays simpler: one price, walkthrough expires, file stays.

Do not discount live. "Live special $9" trains people to wait for you to panic. If you want a live-only extra, make it the walkthrough, not a cheaper file. The file price stays. The show expires.

Worked dollars against the week

Hold the number. Four checkouts at $29 is $116 during the live. Chasing two more by cutting to $9 teaches the room that waiting works. The burst is the point. The page sells the rest of the week at the same price.

The first 72 hours

The first 72 hours assume the pack is already a file you can attach. If it is not, stop and finish the pack. Do not announce a live for a folder of notes.

Day 1 morning: freeze the product

Export the final PDF or zip. Name the file like a human: "Realtor listing pack v1.pdf," not "FINAL_final2." Test-open it on your phone. Write the one-sentence offer. Pick the price. Confirm the Stripe or Stan checkout. Buy it yourself from a second email. If that fails, nothing else in this chapter matters.

Fix the page that looks broken at phone size. If checkout title does not match the pack name, fix it now.

Day 1 afternoon: the first two minutes on a card

Write, on paper you can glance at: hello and how long you will be here; what the file does in one job-shaped sentence; share screen, open the first page, click two things; price and where the link is, said slowly.

Rehearse that out loud twice. Standing up. Do not memorize a speech for minute three through twenty. Human is allowed after the open. The open is not allowed to ramble.

Put the short URL on the same card. Pin-comment draft too.

Day 1 night: calendar and bio

Set the day, clock, timezone on a calendar you will keep. Put the checkout in the bio now. People who cannot attend still need a door. Do not hide the link until you are live. Sleep.

Day 2: announce twice, not twelve

Post the time once in the morning, once in the evening. Example: "Thursday 7pm. I show the file. Link in bio. Twenty minutes." Direct beats a story sticker that expires while they are at dinner.

Tell five people directly. "I'm walking through the listing pack Thursday at 7. Twenty minutes. $29. If that's useful, I'll drop the link when I go live." If someone asks for the link now, send the checkout. The live is not the only door. It is the event.

Do not post twelve countdowns. Two public, five direct.

Day 3: the live and the landing

Hour before: water, charger, Do Not Disturb, link copied, screen ready, second device on orders, notifications off except the platform you are on.

Go live on time. If three people are there, you still start. Demo. Repeat the link. End around minute twenty.

Within two hours: a static page or a pinned post. "Pack is on the page. Walkthrough was tonight." Write three questions you got, one thing you fumbled, the next date or the decision that there is no next date yet. Delivery issues fixed before you sleep.

By hour 72: finished file named like a human, checkout test-bought, first two minutes on a card rehearsed twice, two public announcements, five direct asks, live of twenty minutes, store page the same night.

The path, step by step

Do these in order. Skipping the checkout test is how you host a room and then apologize.

Step 1. Finish one pack

One file, one job, one price. Export, open on a phone, fix the page that looks broken at that size. If you cannot attach it tonight, you do not have a drop. Go back to path 1, 2, 3, or 6. Accountability theater is how you go live with nothing to sell.

Step 2. Set a start time you can keep

Thursday 7pm is a classic. If you work evenings, pick Saturday 10am. Write the timezone. Lock the hour on a calendar. If you cancel dates as a habit, this path will cost you more trust than it makes. Keep the calendar or pick another path.

Step 3. Build the checkout

Title matches the pack. Price is visible. File delivers. Test-buy from a second email. Watch the file arrive. Test on cellular, not only wifi. If this fails, stop. Nothing else matters.

Step 4. Write the first two minutes

Card, not a script deck. Include the screen share in minute two, not minute twelve. Hello, how long, what the file does, open it, price, where the link is. Rehearse twice standing up. The rest can be human.

Step 5. Put the link in bio and in a note you can paste

If you fumble the URL on live, the moment dies. Have a short link written on paper. Pin draft ready. Bio live at least 24 hours before.

Step 6. Announce twice in public and five times in private

Forty-eight hours out, then two hours out. The two-hour reminder fills a small room. Direct DMs to people who already know the job beat a broadcast to strangers. Do not add a 600-word caption that hides the time.

Step 7. Stage the desk

Charged device. A second device on the checkout. Notifications off except the platform you are on. Optional $20 tripod so your demo is not a ceiling fan. Water. Do Not Disturb. The file already open, not buried in eight folders.

Step 8. Go live on time

If three people are there, you still start. Waiting ten minutes for a crowd teaches the three that you do not respect the clock. Start within two minutes of the announced time. You can be a voice and a cursor. You do not need to fake a crowd.

Step 9. Demo, do not lecture

Open the file. Scroll. Fill one example live if you can do it in three minutes. Answer questions about the pack, not your life story. Show the product more than you show your face talking about the product. Do not read comments for ten minutes while the screen is your wallpaper.

Step 10. Repeat the link and the price out loud every three minutes

Pin it. Say it like a person: "Link is in the bio, it's $29, it delivers as soon as you pay." Four times minimum in twenty minutes. People join late. Minute four should still make sense.

Step 11. Close on purpose

At minute twenty, recap what they get, where to buy, and that you are ending. Stay two minutes for last questions. Then leave. Staying until the last person leaves turns a shop into a hangout. Hangouts do not check out.

Step 12. Same night, stand up the store

Replay if you have one. Otherwise a static page: what the pack is, who it is for, price, buy button, "the live walkthrough was [date]." Write the three questions you got. Those become your next post. Fix delivery before you sleep.

Step 13. Do not drop again on adrenaline

Friday Sage does not go live again. You will want to. The algorithm is not the customer. Date the next one when there is a new version, a new sample, or a new audience. Four to six weeks is a rhythm. Tomorrow is a leak.

Step 14. Count, then decide

Peak concurrent, checkouts during plus two hours, page checkouts the rest of the week, questions asked more than once. If you cannot keep dates, stop this path. If live checkouts are zero three times and the page also sells zero, the problem is the pack or the audience, not the lighting.

A worked example: Sage on Thursday at 7

Sage finished a $29 pack on Tuesday night. It is a listing-description stack for solo realtors: twenty-five prompts, three before-and-after listings, a one-page install. PDF plus a short text file. Not a course. A pack.

The date is the product

Sage picks Thursday 7pm Eastern. Twenty minutes. Instagram Live, because that is where the realtor acquaintances already watch Stories. Stan checkout already works — Sage test-bought it last month when the pack sat on a quiet page and sold two copies. Those two copies prove the file delivers. The live is for the rest.

Scarcity is the date. Sage writes: "I walk through the listing pack Thursday at 7. After that, the pack stays $29 on the page. The walkthrough does not." No fake stock. No "only 5 left." The version is v1. Sage will rewrite when realtors actually use it, not because a timer hit zero.

The card and the asks

Tuesday, Sage writes the first two minutes on a yellow pad: "Hey — it's Thursday, I'm here twenty minutes. This is the listing pack I use when a new property hits the MLS and I have twelve minutes before the client wants copy. I'll share my screen, open the PDF, and run one address through the first prompt. Link is in the bio. $29. It delivers immediately."

Sage rehearses that twice in the kitchen. Wednesday: morning Story and evening feed post, same core sentence. Five DMs to agents Sage has actually helped. One person asks for the link now. Sage sends Stan. That buyer pays $29 Wednesday night. The live is not the only door. It is the event.

Thursday 7pm

Phone on a cheap tripod. Charger in. Do Not Disturb except Instagram. Stan open on a tablet. Bio already has the checkout. Pinned comment ready.

At 7:00 Sage goes live with eleven people. Not eleven thousand. Sage does not wait. The card gets through minute two. Screen share. A real listing Sage has permission to show, address blurred. First prompt. Ninety seconds of output. Sage reads two sentences, cuts the fluffy one, shows that edit. That is the demo.

Every three minutes: "Bio has the link. $29. You get the PDF tonight." Someone asks ChatGPT or Claude. Sage answers: both, the install page says how. Someone asks for a discount. Sage says no, nicely. At minute nineteen Sage recaps and ends.

The burst and the recovery

Four checkouts during the live. One more overnight. Wednesday's early buyer makes six packs in two days. $174. Sage puts a static post up at 7:40. Friday Sage does not go live again.

Mistake: Sage almost stayed live until 8:15 because a friend was driving home. Caught it. Ended. Recovery: the friend bought from the static page at 8:22. The date stayed real.

What Sage refused: a countdown sticker that said "3 left." A $9 upsell on the fly. Dual-streaming TikTok. Adding a second product because minute twelve went quiet. Copy the shape, not the niche, unless you also write listings.

Copy you can actually send

Use these as they are. Swap the pack name, the price, the day. Do not add three paragraphs of your origin.

Public post

Thursday 7pm. I show the file. Link in bio. Twenty minutes.

Longer caption: Thursday 7pm Eastern. I walk through the [job] pack on my screen. Twenty minutes, then I leave. $29, instant download. After the live the walkthrough is over; the pack stays on the page.

DM

I'm walking through the [job] pack Thursday at 7. Twenty minutes, $29. If that's useful, I'll have the link in my bio when I go live. If you want it now, here: [checkout]. If not, no need to reply.

Page hero

[Named pack] for [job]. $[price]. Instant download. I walk through it live on [day, time]. After that the walkthrough is gone. The file stays.

Checkout line

$[price]. Instant download of [filename]. The live walkthrough is [day] only. The file is yours either way. Refund if it does not arrive.

Email 1 — 48 hours out

Thursday 7pm Eastern I show the [job] pack on my screen. Twenty minutes. $[price], link in bio the whole time. After the live you can still buy the pack; you miss the walkthrough. If you cannot come, the page is already live: [link].

Email 2 — two-hour reminder

Going live at 7. Twenty minutes. I show the pack, not a slide deck. Link will be in the bio the whole time.

Email 3 — after the live

The walkthrough was tonight. The pack is still $[price] on the page: [link]. Next live is not tomorrow. I'll date the next one when there is a new version worth showing.

Refund

File should have arrived at [email]. If it did not, I just resent it. If you want the money back instead, it is already on the way. I do not haggle the price on live.

The pinned comment

Pack is $[price] — link in bio — delivers the file as soon as you pay. This walkthrough is tonight only.

The two-minute card (read, then demo)

Hey — it's [day], I'm here twenty minutes. This is the [job] pack I use when [specific moment]. I'll share my screen, open the file, and run one example. Link is in the bio. $[price]. It delivers immediately.

What you do not post

Do not post "ONLY 2 SPOTS." Do not post a fake timer. Do not write a 600-word caption that hides the time. Do not post "live special $9."

Week-by-week if you have a job

You do not need a free month. You need three evenings and a Thursday you will not cancel.

Week 1, daily

Day 1: finish the pack. Export. Phone-check. Checkout. Test-buy from a second email. Write the one-sentence offer and the two-minute card. Rehearse twice standing up.

Day 2: announce in the morning and the evening. Five DMs. Bio link live. Calendar locked.

Day 3: go live at the time you promised. Twenty minutes. Static page the same night. Delivery issues fixed before you sleep. Three questions written down.

Day 4: do not drop again. Answer buyer questions. Fix the one page of the PDF that two people could not find.

Day 5–7: ship a quiet v1.1 if it is a real fix, not a reason to go live. Count live checkouts vs page checkouts. Rest.

Week 2, daily

Day 8: one post that teaches a piece of the pack without giving the whole file away. Soft link to the store page.

Day 9–10: answer remaining buyer questions in public if they help the next caption.

Day 11: count sales from the page versus the live. Write the numbers.

Day 12–14: if the live carried it, date the next drop four to six weeks out, not next Thursday. If both live and page are zero, the problem is the pack or the audience. Do not buy a light.

Week 3

Only schedule a second live if you have a new version, a new sample, or a new audience. Repeating the same twenty minutes every week trains people to ignore you. A drop is an event because it is rare.

Use the three questions from week 1 as captions. Keep the store page up. Do not add a membership from the leftover adrenaline.

Week 4

Review: did you keep the date? Average live checkouts. Page checkouts in the following seven days. If you cannot keep dates, stop this path. If you kept the date and sold nothing three times, fix the pack or the room, not the lighting.

Next drop is dated only when there is a reason. Four to six weeks is plenty.

The quality bar

The bar is simple. A tired person who joins at minute four can still tell what the file is, what it costs, and where to buy it.

Below-bar

  • File does not open on a phone, or checkout fails on cellular.
  • You start late. You wait for "more people."
  • Twelve minutes of lecture before the screen share.
  • URL lives only in your head. You fumble it.
  • Fake timer, fake stock, price drop in public.
  • You stay on until the last person leaves.
  • Delivery fails and you sleep anyway.
  • You go live daily, or you cancel twice.
  • You add a second product because the room went quiet.

Above-bar

  • The file opens. The first page states the job.
  • The checkout works on a phone.
  • You can demo without hunting through eight folders.
  • The first two minutes are rehearsed. The rest can be human.
  • You show the product more than you show your face talking about the product.
  • You answer product questions. You do not fake a crowd.
  • You start on time even if the room is small.
  • Price and link every three minutes. End around minute twenty.
  • Buyers get the file before you sleep.
  • Scarcity line is still true in the morning.

Five tests

Test 1, the minute-four joiner. Mute yourself, watch a recording or a rehearsal, join at minute four in your head. Do you know the file, the price, the URL? If not, cut the open.

Test 2, the second-email buy. You already did this, or you did not. If not, do it tonight. Recovery this week: test-buy, fix delivery, then announce.

Test 3, the clock. Did you start within two minutes of the time on the announcement? If not, you taught them your times are decoration. Recovery: the next date is kept or you stop this path.

Test 4, the honest scarcity. Read the announcement the next morning. Is it still true? If you extended, discounted, or restocked a lie, write a true sentence and use only that.

Test 5, the one-file rule. Did a second offer appear because the room was quiet? If yes, you slipped. Recovery: one file on the page. The rest waits for a DM.

If you catch yourself designing a talking-head intro sequence instead of testing the checkout, you have already slipped. Come back to the file and the time.

What to count

Count a few numbers. Do not build a dashboard.

Week 1 / drop day

  • Peak concurrent viewers. For a first drop, 8–40 is a real room. Do not compare this to people with a million followers.
  • Checkouts during the live plus two hours after. That is the burst. First-sale line: at least one from someone who is not you.
  • Checkout test (binary) before you announced.
  • Started on time (binary).
  • Screen share in first three minutes (binary).
  • Questions asked more than once. That is the next caption, or a fix in the file.

Day 30

  • Checkouts the rest of the week from the static page. That tells you if you have a store or only an event.
  • Kept the date (binary). Cancelled lives poison this path.
  • Delivery failures (should be zero).
  • Price held (binary). If you discounted in public, write it down as a miss.
  • v1.1 shipped only for a real fix, not as an excuse to go live again.

Day 90 / after three drops

Write down: average live checkouts, average page checkouts in the following seven days, and whether you kept the date. If you cannot keep dates, stop this path. If live checkouts are zero three times and the page also sells zero, the problem is the pack or the audience, not the lighting.

Cadence: drops four to six weeks apart, each with a reason.

Ignore

Ignore likes on the announcement. Ignore whether a stranger from a Facebook group said they would come. Ignore your heart rate. Ignore a view count that includes people who stayed for four seconds. Ignore dual-stream vanity. Ignore "the algorithm wants daily."

One-line spreadsheet

Date | kept clock (Y/N) | peak viewers | live+2h checkouts | page checkouts 7d | price held (Y/N) | delivery fails | three questions | next date or none

One row per drop. If you need a funnel dashboard, you are avoiding the demo.

Objections you will hear — including your own

"Nobody will show up."

Maybe. You still go live at the time you announced if even one person is there. A cancelled live teaches your small audience that your times are decoration. Reply to yourself: "I demo for three. I keep the date. The page still goes up."

"I hate being on camera."

Share the screen. Pin the product. You can be a voice and a cursor. Rehearse the two minutes so you are not staring at your own face looking for a personality. Reply: "They came for the file. The cursor is enough."

"Live selling is slimy."

Fake stock is slimy. A date and a demo are a shop hours sign. You are allowed to say the price out loud. You are not allowed to invent a shortage. Reply: "The walkthrough expires. The file stays. That is a shop sign, not a trick."

"I'll go live when I have more followers."

Eight people who already trust you will buy more than eight hundred cold viewers. Get the pack right. Date the drop. Reply: "Eleven is a room. Two quiet sales already proved delivery. Thursday stands."

"Someone asked for a discount on the live."

Say the price again. Offer the static page if they need to think. Do not negotiate in public. If you made a real error in the file, refund, do not haggle. Reply: "It's $29. Link in bio. If you need to think, the page stays."

"What if they buy and want a course?"

You sold a pack. Point them to the page. A setup session is path 20, priced separately, not a surprise at minute sixteen. Reply: "This is the pack. Setup is a different product with a date. I can send that after."

"What if the checkout breaks during the live?"

Have the URL on paper. Have a backup payment link. If both fail, stop selling, take names, deliver by hand that night. Fix the pipe before you announce another Thursday. Reply: "I'm stopping the buy button until it works. If you comment your email, you get the file tonight."

"Should I go live every day to feed the algorithm?"

No. Date the next one when you have a reason: a new version, a new sample, a real cohort. Reply: "A drop is rare on purpose. Daily is how people learn to ignore me."

"Can I use a fake timer if everyone does it?"

No. Scarcity is a date, a cohort, or a version. Fake stock on a digital file is how you teach buyers to ignore you. Reply: "I will not lie about a PDF."

"What if only my mom shows up?"

You demo. You keep the date. You still put the store page up. Sage's first useful room was eleven. Yours can be smaller. Reply: "Three is a room. I start."

What this feeds — and what feeds it

Upstream — what must exist first

Live drops are not a first path. They are an amplifier. You need a pack from path 1, 2, 3, 6, or 9. A live with nothing to sell is a talk show. Finish the file. Then drop it.

A checkout that already delivered at least once. Quiet sales are the proof. If you have never test-bought, you are early.

One platform where a few dozen people already watch. Not two. One.

Downstream — what this feeds

The static store. People who missed Thursday still need a button.

Your list, if you collect emails on the checkout. Do not build a 12-email sequence before you have a live that works.

Proof. A screen recording of you opening your own product is more useful than a designed ad. That clip can become a caption, a page header, or the next announcement.

Questions from the live become posts and, if they repeat, a v1.1 of the file.

A service path, later, in the DMs, for the buyer who asks for you to run it. Not in minute twelve.

What not to chain on night one

Do not launch a membership from the live. Do not pitch an automation setup. Do not read a menu of twelve offers. One file. After the burst, you can point a buyer who asks for more toward a service path — in the DMs, not in minute twelve.

Do not chain a second live on Friday. Adrenaline is not a calendar.

Mistakes that kill a drop

Lying about stock. Reading comments and never showing the product. Going live daily until nobody cares. Those three still kill it. Here is the rest, with recovery this week.

1. Going live with a draft

Promising a zip you have not exported. Recovery this week: export, phone-check, test-buy. Cancel any announced live that has no file. Re-date after the pipe works.

2. Changing the price mid-live

The room is small, so you panic to $9. Recovery this week: hold $29. If you already dropped it, do not do it again. Write the number on the card.

3. Adding a second product because the room went quiet

Now nobody knows what to buy. Recovery this week: one file on the page. The rest waits.

4. Starting late / waiting for more people

You teach the three that the clock is decoration. Recovery this week: start within two minutes even if the room is one person.

5. Lecturing for twelve minutes before the screen share

They came for the file. Recovery this week: screen share in minute two. Put it on the card.

6. Fumbling the URL

It lived only in your head. Recovery this week: short link on paper, pin ready, bio live 24 hours before.

7. Staying on until the last person leaves

The night becomes a hangout. Recovery this week: recap at minute twenty, two minutes of questions, leave.

8. Fake countdown timers and "only 3 left"

Fake stock on a PDF. Recovery this week: delete the sticker. Scarcity is the date, the cohort, or the version. Write one true sentence.

9. A live every day, or a live you cancel twice

Cadence mistakes. Recovery this week: one dated drop. If you already cancelled, apologize once, pick a date you will keep, or stop this path.

10. No store page afterward

Anyone who hears about it on Friday has nowhere to go. Recovery this week: static page or pinned post within two hours of ending, even after a quiet room.

11. Delivery fails and you sleep

Trust dies overnight. Recovery this week: fix before you sleep. Resend. Refund if you cannot deliver.

12. Dual-streaming a first drop

Two comment threads, two bios, one confused host. Recovery this week: one room. One link.

13. Announcing before the checkout works

You host a room and then apologize. Recovery this week: test-buy first, announce second. Always that order.

Tools — only what you need

You need a place to go live, a place to get paid, and a card for the first two minutes.

Exact stack

  • TikTok Live or Instagram Live. Pick the one where your people already are. Do not dual-stream a first drop. One room, one comment thread, one bio link. YouTube Live is fine if that is your actual home. Zoom is a meeting, not a drop, unless you already sell into a private list and sent a calendar hold.
  • Stan, Stripe Payment Link, or Gumroad. One product. The link must be short enough to say out loud. Test on cellular, not only wifi.
  • A charger. A second screen or a tablet for orders. A notes app with the URL and the price.
  • Optional: a $20 tripod so your demo is not a ceiling fan.
  • Paper card for the first two minutes.

Setup order

  1. Export the pack. Phone-check.
  2. Checkout. Test-buy from a second email.
  3. Write the two-minute card. Rehearse twice.
  4. Bio link live.
  5. Calendar the hour.
  6. Announce twice public, five direct.
  7. Stage the desk. Then go live.
  8. Static page the same night.

What not to buy

Do not add a webinar platform, a registration funnel, a wait-room video, or an on-air producer. Those are for people who already sell out rooms. You are dating a Thursday. Do not buy lights, a second camera, or a stream deck for drop one. Do not buy ads to fill a first room of eleven.

The $0 path

Phone you already have. Instagram or TikTok you already have. A Stripe or Stan or Gumroad link you already used for the quiet page. Paper for the card. A stack of books as a stand if you have no tripod. Free pinned post as the store. This is enough. Sage's tripod was cheap, not required. The bottleneck is the finished file and the kept time.

Checklist

Print this or copy it into a note. Check boxes in order.

  • Pack is exported and opens on a phone
  • Filename is human
  • First page of the file states the job
  • One price, written: $19, $29, $39, or $47
  • Checkout title matches the pack
  • Checkout test-bought from a second email; file arrived
  • Tested on cellular, not only wifi
  • One-sentence offer written
  • Scarcity line is a date, a cohort, or a version (one)
  • First two minutes on a card, rehearsed twice out loud
  • Short URL written on paper
  • Day, clock time, and timezone on a calendar
  • Bio link live at least 24 hours before
  • Two public announcements: 48 hours out, 2 hours out
  • Five direct messages to people who already know the job
  • Device charged, Do Not Disturb on, second device on the order screen
  • File already open, not buried in folders
  • Start on time even if the room is small
  • Screen share in the first three minutes
  • Price and link said every three minutes
  • End around minute twenty
  • Static page or pinned post up within two hours
  • Delivery issues fixed before you sleep
  • Three questions written down
  • No second live scheduled on adrenaline
  • Spreadsheet row: peak, live checkouts, page checkouts, clock kept

FAQ

How long should I stay live?

Twenty minutes. Twenty-five if questions are about the file. Not an hour. Default: twenty, then leave.

What if only three people show up?

You demo for three. You keep the date. You still put the store page up. Sage's first useful room was eleven. Yours can be smaller. Default: start anyway.

TikTok or Instagram?

Whichever already has your people. If both are empty, this is not your first path. Build a pack and a small audience on one platform, then drop. Default: one platform you already open.

Do I have to show my face?

No. Show the file. A stable screen and a clear voice beat a nervous talking head that never shares the product. Default: screen first, face optional.

Can I use a fake timer if "everyone does it"?

No. Scarcity is a date, a cohort, or a version. Fake stock on a digital file is how you teach buyers to ignore you. Default: date only, unless you have a real cohort cap.

Should I go live every day to feed the algorithm?

No. Date the next one when you have a reason: a new version, a new sample, a real cohort. Default: four to six weeks, with a reason.

What if the checkout breaks during the live?

Have the URL on paper. Have a backup payment link. If both fail, stop selling, take names, deliver by hand that night. Fix the pipe before you announce another Thursday. Default: stop selling, deliver by hand, fix, then re-date.

Do I need a replay?

Nice if the platform gives you one. Not required. The static page is required. The live is the event. The page is the store. Default: page same night, replay if cheap.

Can I drop a pack I did not finish because "the live will hold me accountable"?

No. Finish the pack first. Accountability theater is how you go live with nothing to sell. Default: export, test-buy, then announce.

What should I charge if my pack already sells at $19 on the page?

Keep $19, or use the live to introduce a $29 version that actually added examples. Do not raise the price only because you turned a camera on. Default: keep $19 unless the version is real.

What if someone wants a discount in the comments?

Say the price again. Offer the page if they need to think. Do not negotiate in public. Default: no discount, ever, on live.

Zoom or Instagram Live?

Instagram or TikTok if the people already watch there. Zoom only if you have a private list and a calendar hold. Default: the app they already open.

Can I sell a $197 pack on a first live?

Live does not make a high ticket feel cheap. Default: $19–$47. High ticket is another path.

What if I freeze on camera?

Card for two minutes, then screen share. You can be a voice and a cursor. Default: rehearse twice standing up; share the file by minute two.

How many DMs is too many?

Five direct asks to people who know the job. Not fifty cold pitches. Default: five.

When is the next drop?

When there is a new version, a new sample, or a new audience. Not tomorrow. Default: date it four to six weeks out, or do not date it yet.

PATH 18

Research and brief service

A messy question in. A two-page brief out. You verify what the model cannot know.
