Week-by-week if you have a job

You can do this around a job if you protect two evenings and one 45-minute screen share. The goal of the first month is three setups a stranger can use without you.

Week 1

Day 1: sample project for a job you know, tested, plus the five-minute walkthrough. Fake files only.

Day 2: page with a $197 button. Test-buy from a second email. Intake questions on the page.

Day 3: three asks to people who already pay for the model.

Day 4: two more asks. Do not design a catalog of twelve industries.

Day 5: if a yes arrives, schedule intake after they can log in. Do not start in your account.

Day 6–7: deliver the first paid setup if the calendar says so, or rest. Do not start a "hosted GPT" idea because someone asked.

Week 2

Day 8–9: install in their account. They click. They run a starter without you typing. Walkthrough sent. Tweak window in writing.

Day 10: delete their files from your machine. Write the intake as a form.

Day 11–14: one tweak if they ask. Viewer access ends. You leave. Two more asks if you have no second buyer.

Week 3

Two more asks, or a second paid setup at $197. Same ownership rules. If nobody buys, the job is too vague or you asked strangers who do not already pay for the model. Sell to people who already have the subscription. You are not also selling them Claude.

Week 4

Third setup or stop. Log fees, "ran without you," tweaks that were actually a second job. If three clients needed the same shape, note it for a later skill pack with generic files. Do not mix that pack with this custom setup. Ask once whether they still open the project. If they never opened it, you overbuilt or you sold a course to a person who wanted a lecture.

The quality bar

The bar is use-without-you. Pretty instructions that nobody runs are a brochure. Volume of knowledge files is not quality. Jules's bookkeeper project used phrases, not a dump of five years of returns.

Below the bar

  • Project in your account.
  • 2,000-word role-play they are afraid to edit.
  • Starters that only work if you are typing.
  • A 40-minute "training" instead of a five-minute walkthrough.
  • Confidential files they did not approve.
  • Forty folders they will never open.
  • Selling access to Claude as if you were the vendor.
  • Automations bundled into the $197.
  • Copies of their files on your machine after hand-off.
  • You still admin after day eight.

Above the bar

  • Their account. They clicked.
  • Instructions under a page: role, inputs, output, missing-info, do-not-invent.
  • Three named starters that produce a draft a human would edit.
  • Approved files only, small, dated.
  • Five-minute walkthrough that shows ownership and how to edit you out.
  • They run a starter without you typing.
  • Seven-day tweak, then closed.
  • Your access gone. Their files gone from your machine.

Five tests before you leave

  1. The log-out test. You are not in the room. They run starter two.
  2. The edit test. They change one instruction line and it still works.
  3. The missing-info test. You leave a number out. It asks. It does not invent.
  4. The file test. Nothing in the project that they did not approve.
  5. The five-minute test. The walkthrough is five minutes. If you need twelve, you built too much.

If you fail one test, you are not handed off. You fix it inside the sitting or inside the tweak window. You do not "stay as admin until they are comfortable." Comfort is them clicking, not you owning.

What to count

Count a short list. File counts are vanity. Jules used phrases, not a dump.

Week 1

  • Sample project tested: yes or no.
  • Five-minute walkthrough recorded: yes or no.
  • $197 button test-bought: yes or no.
  • Asks sent: target 5.
  • Paid setups: target 1. A sample in your account is not a sale.

Day 30

  • Setups handed off: target 3.
  • They ran a starter without you: yes or no. That is the first-sale definition.
  • Tweak requests that are actually a second job. Those mean intake was soft.
  • Time from intake to hand-off. Target: inside a week, often one sitting plus the recording.
  • Average fee. If you are stuck at $97 after five, press $197 and live with fewer yeses.
  • Your access removed: yes or no.

Day 90

  • How many still open the project two weeks later — ask once. If they never opened it, you overbuilt or you sold a course.
  • Stranger sales: at least 1.
  • Fee at $197 or $297, not $97.
  • Zero hosted GPTs.
  • Intake lives in a form.
  • One note about a generic skill pack, if three clients needed the same shape. Not built yet unless the custom work is boring in a good way.

If day 90 is empty, you asked people who do not pay for the model, or you never sent the five asks. Stop adding files to the sample. Send the sentence.

Ignore

How many knowledge files you uploaded. How long the instructions are past one page. Time spent naming a "studio." Compliments that are not a starter they ran.

One-line spreadsheet

Date | job in five words | fee | they ran starter without you Y/N | tweak was second job Y/N | access removed Y/N | still opening it two weeks later Y/N

That is the whole system.

Objections you will hear — including your own

Reply once. Do not hold a prompt-engineering seminar in the thread.

"They could watch a YouTube video."

They could. They have not. You are selling a configured job in their account in a week, not a lecture.

"Isn't this just writing a prompt?"

A prompt they have to paste every time is not a project. Instructions plus files plus three working threads is a small appliance. Price the appliance.

"They want it in my account so they don't have to pay for Claude."

No. That is selling access to a model you do not own. They need their own subscription. You configure it. If they will not pay the model, they will not pay you fairly either.

"What about confidential files?"

Follow their policy. When in doubt, do not upload. Paste per chat. Write that in the intake. Loading their client list into a project "to be helpful" is how you get a story you do not want.

"Can I productize one project and sell access to many buyers?"

That is a skill pack (path 2), with generic files, not their confidential ones. Different product. Do not mix a custom setup with a shared GPT you rent out.

"Is $197 too low?"

It is a setup, not a month of service. If they want weekly-run work, sell path 7. If the setup is truly two jobs and picky files, $297. Do not raise to $1,000 for instructions.

"Can I do this over email only?"

Yes, if they write a clear intake. Live screen share is faster for hand-off. Jules uses twenty minutes live plus the recording. Default: live for job one.

"They want me to stay as admin."

No. Viewer for seven days if it helps them sleep. Then you leave. Ownership is the product. If they are afraid to click, the walkthrough failed. Fix the walkthrough, do not take the keys.

"What if the model changes next month?"

You guarantee a working configuration at hand-off and one tweak week. After that, they own the maintenance, or they buy another setup. You do not guarantee output quality forever.

"I don't have five people who pay for Claude."

Then this is not your first path this month. Sell a playbook or a service to people you already know, then offer setups to the ones who already have the subscription.

What this feeds — and what feeds it

Hand off. The best compliment is a week of silence because they are using it.

What feeds a $197 setup

People who already pay for Claude or ChatGPT and stall on the blank project. Buyers of a skill pack who want it installed. Service clients who keep asking you to "just set up the GPT." Your own sample and walkthrough. A brief (path 18) whose next step was "configure the tool," quoted separately.

People who do not pay for the model are not feedstock. You are not the vendor.

What a setup feeds

  • Skill packs, if three clients needed the same shape. Generic version, no client files, sold as a file.
  • Automations, if they then want the project to draft from a form. New quote. Path 19.
  • A productized service, if they want you to run the job, not own the tool.
  • Another $197 setup for a second job, after the first is in their account and used.
  • Not a hosted model business. That is the thing you leave alone.

What not to feed

Do not feed a membership that is actually access to your account. Do not feed a staff workshop into the $197. Do not use their files as the next sample. Do not turn the seven-day tweak window into a weekly run of the job.

Mistakes that kill this path

Keeping the project in your account. Loading their confidential files into a model against their policy. Overbuilding a second brain they will never open. Those three still kill it. The rest kill it more slowly.

Ten mistakes and the recovery this week

  1. Keeping the project in your account. Recovery: copy the text into theirs on a screen share today. Remove yourself. If they will not pay for the model, refund and stop.
  1. Loading confidential files they did not approve. Recovery: delete from the project and from your machine today. Tell them. Paste-per-chat from now on.
  1. Overbuilding a second brain. Recovery: cut to three starters and the files they will use this week. Archive the rest. Re-record five minutes.
  1. Writing instructions they are afraid to edit. Recovery: cut to under a page. Role, inputs, output, missing-info, do-not-invent. Have them change one line with you watching.
  1. Starters that only work if you are typing. Recovery: log out. Watch them run starter two. Rewrite the starter until they can.
  1. A 40-minute "training" instead of a five-minute walkthrough. Recovery: record five minutes tonight. Send that. Do not schedule a webinar.
  1. Selling access to Claude as if you were the vendor. Recovery: take the page down. Refund anyone in your account. Configure theirs or stop.
  1. Bundling automations into the $197. Recovery: finish the setup only. Quote path 19 separately. Do not keep building pipes inside this fee.
  1. Keeping copies of their files "for examples." Recovery: delete them today. Use your fake sample for the portfolio.
  1. Staying admin after day eight because they asked. Recovery: drop to viewer, then leave. Fix the walkthrough if they are scared. Do not take the keys.
  1. Asking people who do not pay for the model. Recovery: rewrite the five names. Only subscribers. You are not selling Claude.
  1. Discounting to $20 because it "felt like a prompt." Recovery: next button is $197. A prompt they paste is not this product.

If you catch yourself in any of these, the recovery is this week. Ownership and files do not wait until you "have a process."

Tools — only what you need

Claude Projects or Custom GPTs. One. The five-minute walkthrough: QuickTime, Loom, or your phone pointed at the screen, as long as they can hear you and see the clicks. Configure the tool they already open.

Exact stack

  • Claude Projects or Custom GPTs, whichever they already pay for.
  • A page with a $197 button (Stan, Stripe Payment Link, Gumroad — one).
  • An intake form: job, tone samples, files allowed, policy notes.
  • Stripe or Stan. Test-buy from a second email.
  • A calendar slot of 45 minutes if you do intake live, or the form if they write clearly.
  • Screen share for the install (their tool, not yours).
  • A place to send the five-minute recording they own.

Setup order

  1. Sample project for a job you know, tested.
  2. Five-minute walkthrough.
  3. $197 button, test-confirmed.
  4. Intake questions written.
  5. Five asks.
  6. Live install in their account.
  7. They run a starter.
  8. Walkthrough sent, tweak window in writing.
  9. Access removed, their files deleted from your machine.

What not to buy

Do not build a native app. Do not resell API access. Do not stand up a team workspace they do not need. Do not buy a "GPT store" plan that is actually you hosting. Do not add an automation platform inside this fee. Do not buy a course on prompt empires.

The $0 path

A Claude or ChatGPT account you already pay for, used only to build the sample, never to host theirs. A Google Doc as the "page" with a payment link you already have. Loom free, or your phone. A Google Form for intake. The $0 path is allowed for the first setup. It is not an excuse to host them in your login or to skip the walkthrough.

Checklist

  • Sample project for a job you know, tested
  • Fake files in the sample, no client data
  • Five-minute walkthrough recorded
  • $197 button on a page, test-confirmed
  • Five asks to people who already pay for the model
  • Intake: job, tone, allowed files, data policy
  • They have their own paid account before you start
  • Project created in their account
  • They click the buttons
  • Instructions they can read and edit, under a page
  • Missing-info rule and do-not-invent rule
  • Three named starter threads that already work
  • No confidential files they did not approve
  • They run a starter without you typing
  • Walkthrough delivered
  • Seven-day tweak window in writing
  • Tweak means instructions and starters, not a second job
  • Your access removed
  • Their files deleted from your machine
  • You said out loud: you are not reselling the model
  • No $19/month access to your GPT
  • Automations quoted separately if they ask
  • One-line spreadsheet row filled
  • Viewer, if any, ends on day eight
  • Portfolio uses the fake sample only

FAQ

Claude Project or Custom GPT?

Whichever they already pay for and open. If they use both, pick the one for this job. Do not configure two for $197. Default: their daily tool.

What if they do not have a paid account?

They need one. You do not sell them yours. Send the signup link. Schedule the setup after they can log in. Default: no install until they can click.

Can I do this over email only?

Yes, if they write a clear intake. Live screen share is faster for hand-off. Jules uses twenty minutes live plus the recording. Default: live for the first three jobs.

How long should instructions be?

Short enough they will edit them. Usually under a page. If you need four pages, you are writing a playbook (path 1) and calling it a project. Default: under a page.

What goes in the three starters?

The three jobs they will actually run this week. Not edge cases. Not "tell me about yourself." Named, boring, useful. Default: three jobs they named in intake.

Is $197 too low?

It is a setup, not a month of service. If they want weekly-run work, sell path 7. If the setup is truly two jobs and picky files, $297. Default: $197 until five setups say otherwise.

What is the tweak window for?

Instruction and starter fixes. Not "also build my content engine." Write that down. Default: seven days, one tweak.

Can I show their project as a case study?

Only with permission, and never with their files. Show your sample instead. Jules shows the fake receivables list. Default: fake sample only.

Do I guarantee output quality forever?

No. Models change. You guarantee a working configuration at hand-off and one tweak week. After that, they own the maintenance, or they buy another setup. Default: no forever.

What if they ask me to stay as admin?

No. Viewer for seven days if it helps them sleep. Then you leave. Ownership is the product. Default: leave.

Can I keep a copy of the instructions I wrote?

The generic shape, yes. Their tone samples and files, no. Default: delete their materials from your machine on hand-off.

Should I configure both Claude and ChatGPT?

Not for $197. One platform, the one they open. A second platform is a second setup at $197 or a $297 two-job quote, written. Default: one.

What if they want forty knowledge files?

No. Small set they will maintain. A second brain they will never open is a mistake, not a bonus. Default: only approved, small, dated files.

Can this replace a productized service?

No. This is configuration. Running the job every week is path 7. If they ask you to stay and write the emails, quote the service. Default: do not run the job inside the setup fee.

When do I turn this into a skill pack?

After three clients needed the same shape. Generic files. No confidential anything. Different page, different product. Default: not after one setup.

What the door actually is

Definition

A front door is a useful diagnostic. Seven questions. They get a score and one next step. You get an email. The free file is useful even if they never buy. That is the deal you keep.

This suite is The Operator Suite. You may brand your own scorecard. You may not copy this book, sell it as yours, or give it away as if you wrote it. Build your door. Point it at your playbook.

The door is seven questions a tired person will finish on a phone, a two-to-four page PDF that still helps if they never pay you, and a 5-7 note sequence that teaches, then asks. Friends and DMs got you the first sales. The door is how people you have never met join that line without you hunting each one by hand.

What it is not

It is not a 14-page free guide that is a sales letter with a checklist slapped on page 13. It is not this suite with your name on the cover. It is not a 40-field form that feels like a job application. It is not a fake score that always says you need my $47 file.

If they can tell, in two minutes, that the PDF only exists to sell, you built a flyer. Flyers do not earn replies from strangers. Diagnostics do. It is not a webinar, a 12-email course, or a community. Those can come later.

Why email is required

A stranger who takes a score and disappears was never going to buy this week. That is fine. The door still has to be fair: they get the file instantly. You get a way to teach for a few notes, then ask. No hostage PDF. No we will send it someday. Instant, then a sequence that earns the ask.

Email is not a trick. It is the only address you control. A like, a follow, a comment — those live on someone else's platform. When the algorithm changes, you have nothing. The list is the asset this path builds. The score is how you earn the address without lying. Require the email. Include an unsubscribe. Both.

Why a diagnostic beats a PDF dump

People will not finish a 40-page free book they did not ask for. They will finish seven questions if each one feels like it is about them. A score gives them language for a problem they already have. That language is what they carry into the paid playbook later.

A dump of chapters from a book you did not write is theft and it is also bad marketing. Nobody finishes it. The scorecard you actually wrote for one job will outperform a stolen encyclopedia every week of the year.

Seven is the number because it is enough to change the advice and short enough to finish on a phone. Five can work. Forty cannot. Multiple choice only.

Why this works now

Attention is expensive. Ads into a sales page with no list behind it burn cash. AI made generic lead magnets free and useless. The remaining gap is a diagnostic that uses the language of one job. AI readiness quiz is wallpaper. Seven questions for a one-person landscaping company that wants a week of posts is a door. Strangers already took a dozen quizzes that spat out 94 out of 100 and a pitch. Three honest bands and one free action still feel like a person.

Anti-pattern 1: the brochure

Page one is your bio. Page two is a story. Page three is a pitch. The score is a sticker. Recovery: delete pages one through three. Lead with the band meanings and one free action. Your name belongs in the footer as a human, not as a keynote on page one. The PDF is a diagnostic, not a memoir.

Anti-pattern 2: the hostage file

Enter your email and we will send it in 24 hours so we can nurture you. They already did the work of answering. Pay them immediately with the file. Nurture after they have it.

Instant means on the thank-you screen and in the first email. Not check your promotions tab in a few hours while we wait to look hungry. If your tool cannot attach a PDF on submit, link the file on the next screen and send the same link in note 1. Two minutes, not two days.

Anti-pattern 3: passing this book off as yours

You export this suite, slap your logo on the cover, and call it a magnet. That is passing this book off as yours. It is off limits. It also trains buyers to see you as a reseller. Write a scorecard. Point at your playbook. That is the work. If you are unsure whether a file you are about to publish is yours, it is not. Write seven questions for one job. That file is yours.

The deal you keep

They get a real next step they can do this week without paying you. You get an email and permission to send a short sequence. You do not get a right to spam daily, sell them twelve things in note one, or republish someone else's book. If you cannot keep that deal, do not publish the form.

Who this is for — and who should skip it

This path fits if you finished any earlier path. You have something to point at — usually path 1, a playbook — and you need people you have never met. Friends and DMs got you the first sales. The door is how strangers join that line without you hunting each one.

Fits if

You can write seven questions that change the advice. If every answer leads to buy my file, the questions are fake.

You can write a two-to-four page PDF that still helps if they never pay you. You will set up a 5-7 note sequence before you buy a single ad. You already have a named paid next step with a live checkout you have test-bought from a second email. You will require an email and include an unsubscribe. Both. Not one. You will write your own scorecard, not paste this book into a PDF with your name on it.

Skip if

Skip it if you have nothing to sell yet. A door into an empty house is a hobby. Skip it if you planned to republish this suite as your lead magnet. Skip it if you will not include an unsubscribe. Skip it if you want a list more than you want to be useful — that motive leaks onto page one.

Skip it if you need cash this week. Send ten more personal messages for the file you already have. The door is a stranger machine. It is not a substitute for asking people who already know you.

Skip it if you will not test delivery from a second inbox. A form that looks live and never sends the PDF is how you teach strangers to ignore you.

The honest middle

If the playbook is 80 percent done and the checkout works, you may write the questions now and finish the PDF on the same weekend. You may not launch the form pointing at a playbook you have not exported.

If you have a skill pack and no playbook, the door can point at the skill pack. Pick one paid thing. Write it on a sticky note so the sequence does not wander into a buffet.

If you have done the job for two local owners and you have notes, those notes are the playbook. Finish that file. Then the door. You do not need a following. You need one paid next step, seven honest questions, and a room you already help enough to share once.

Skills and time

You need seven multiple-choice questions, a scoring key, a two-to-four page PDF, a form in Tally or Beehiiv, and 5-7 short notes. None of that is code. You need a second email so you can take the form as a stranger. You need a friend who does the job, for the fairness test.

Time: two evenings for questions plus PDF, one evening for the form and the test, one evening for the sequence. Share once the next morning. If you only have 40 minutes a night, spread that same work across seven nights. Do not buy ads to skip the writing. Budget: $0 if you use Google Docs, a free form, and a free MailerLite or Beehiiv tier.

Two-minute self-test

Answer these out loud. If you stall on any of them, you are not ready for the door this week.

  • What is the paid file or service a stranger would buy after the sequence? Name the title and the price.
  • Can a friend take one useful action from a two-page PDF without paying you? What is that action, in one sentence?
  • Will you write the 5-7 notes before you share the form? Yes or no.
  • Are you willing to require an email, and to let them leave in one click? Yes or no.
  • Will you write your own scorecard, and not paste this book into a PDF with your name on it? Yes or no.

Five yeses. Then start Day 1. Four or fewer: finish the missing piece first.

The stranger on the other side

They are not a fan. They found a post in a group, or a link under a comment you left that actually helped. They have four minutes on a phone. They will finish seven questions if the first one sounds like their Tuesday. They will bounce at question two if you got cute. They will buy later only if the free action worked. Write for that person. Not for a marketer who collects magnets.

The offer, named in one sentence

Seven questions. A score. One next step. Free even if you never buy.

That is the public offer. The private truth: the sequence teaches, then sells path 1. Both can be true if the PDF is real.

Fill this before you outline

I help [specific person] see [named situation] in seven questions, and I give them [one free action] even if they never buy. The paid next step is [playbook title] at [price].

If you cannot fill those brackets, you do not have a door. You have a vibe. Specific person is a job plus a constraint. Named situation is something they already feel on a Tuesday. One free action is a 20-minute task that does not need a card. Paid next step is one product, one price. Not a buffet.

Put the filled sentence at the top of the Doc that will become the PDF. If you need and to name the person or the paid thing, you have two doors. Pick one.

Sentences that work

  • Seven questions for one-person landscapers who want a week of posts. A score. One action you can do tonight. Free even if you never buy the 10-day file.
  • A 7-question AI-readiness scorecard for solo bookkeepers. Instant PDF. One close-the-month action that does not require a new subscription.
  • Clinic front-desk diagnostic: seven questions, a score, one reminder-text you can send this week. No pitch on page one.
  • For tutors who freeze at lesson notes. Seven questions. A band. One template to try on Thursday. The paid pack is later, if you want it.
  • Trades AI scorecard. Seven questions. One next step. Built for people who hate forms and will bounce if this feels like a trap.

Write yours in that shape. One person. Seven questions. One free action. One paid file named, not pitched on page one.

What they get

  • Seven questions, scored honestly.
  • A PDF that explains the score in plain language and gives one next step they can do this week without paying you.
  • Instant delivery. The file is in the thank-you email or the next screen, not in a queue you will get to.
  • A short sequence they can leave in one click.
  • Three bands, not a fake 94 out of 100. A sentence per band a skeptical friend would accept.

What they do not get

They do not get this suite. They do not get a fake 94 out of 100. They do not get a 40-page book you copied. They do not get daily pitches. They do not get a webinar they have to sit through to see the score. They do not get a community invite in note 1. They do not get The Operator Suite with your sticker on the cover.

Packaging

The public name is a scorecard for a job, with your name, not the name of this book. Example: Trades AI scorecard — Noor. Two to four pages. Your email in the footer as a human. Year on the cover. A sentence that the file is free even if they never buy.

Filename a tired person can find later: trades-ai-scorecard-noor.pdf. Cover states the job, the seven questions, and that it is free. No fake 94 in a circle.

The four layers

The form is the product's front. The PDF is the gift. The sequence is the relationship. The playbook is the ask. Keep those four layers in that order.

If you reverse them — ask on the form, pitch in the PDF, teach never — you built a flyer with extra fields. Strangers can tell. They leave at question two, or they take the file and mute you. Keep the order. The ask waits for notes 5-7.

The public name of the door is a job plus the word scorecard plus you. Do not put this book's title on their PDF. Do not put this book's chapter list in their magnet. Do not give this book away as if you wrote it.

What done looks like

Definition

Done is the first email from someone you have never met, sitting in a tool you control, with a score attached, and a PDF they already received. The sequence exists. Unsubscribe works. The paid playbook is linked in a later note, not in the first paragraph of the free file. The scorecard is a file you wrote, not this suite with a sticker on it.

The fairness test

Give the PDF to a friend and tell them not to buy anything. If they can still take one useful action this week, the door is honest. If they cannot, you wrote a sales letter and called it a scorecard. Rewrite until the friend has a next step that does not require a card.

Run the test twice. Once with a friend who does the job. Once with a friend who does not. The first friend should nod. The second friend should still understand the action even if they will never do it. If the second friend is lost, the PDF is inside-baseball. Plain it out.

Do not hover. Hand them the file. Sit in another room. Ask one question when they are done: what would you do this week, in one sentence. If they say buy your thing, you failed. If they name the free action, you passed.

Technical done

  • Form live. Email required. Seven questions. No 40 fields.
  • PDF attached or linked immediately on the thank-you screen and in note 1.
  • Confirmation they expect. From-name they recognize.
  • Sequence of 5-7 notes drafted, not I will write them when people join.
  • Unsubscribe one click, tested.
  • Path 1 checkout test-bought from a second email. The sequence must not point at a dead button.
  • You filled the form as a stranger from a second inbox and received the file in under two minutes.
  • Privacy line under the button, one sentence: you are joining a short sequence, you can leave in one click.

Not done yet

A Google Doc of questions with no scoring key. A PDF that mentions the paid file more than the free action. A sequence outline with no actual sentences. A plan to write the notes after the first ten people join. Those are sketches. Sketches are not a door. A tagging architecture, a webinar date, an ad account — those wait.

The first-sale definition on this path

The first sale is the first email from someone you have never met. Cash from the playbook is path 1 using the door. Count both. Do not pretend the list is failing because the $29 did not happen on day one. The address is the win this path is built to get. Write the date, the source, and the score band on one line.

The second-inbox night

Before you share, open a browser you do not usually use. A second Gmail. Fill the form as if you were suspicious and tired. Submit. Start a timer. The file should be on the next screen. Note 1 should arrive. The PDF should open on a phone. Unsubscribe should be one click and should actually leave. Click the playbook link in note 5 as a draft — the checkout should take a test-buy you already did.

If any of that fails, you are not done. Fix it before one stranger sees the form. A broken first impression is expensive. You will not get that stranger back.

Pricing — the door is free, the house is not

The door is free

The cash window is not a price on the PDF. The door feeds every other path. You do not charge for the seven questions. Free means free. Useful means useful without a receipt. If you cannot stand that, this is not your path this month. Go sell the playbook with ten more personal messages.

Do not charge $9 for the scorecard and also call it free. Do not put a tripwire on a diagnostic. The tripwire path is a different product. This path is a door. Doors do not have a cover charge.

Where money shows up

  • Path 1 playbook, usually $19-$47, asked for in note 5, 6, or 7 after you have taught.
  • Later: a service, a setup, a drop. Not in the first email.
  • Optional: a $97-$197 live walkthrough of their results, sold as itself, after they already have the PDF. Do not hide that inside the magnet.

The sequence may sell one named thing. Write that thing on a sticky note. If note 6 starts selling a second product, you wandered. Put the second product in a later letter, after this sequence ends.

Worked dollars

Twenty strangers finish the form in a month. Sequence is live. Two buy the $29 playbook. That is $58, which is not the point. You now have twenty addresses you can tell about a Thursday drop, a skill pack, or a setup. The next 90 days is where the door pays. If you judge this path on week-one cash, you will kill it and go back to hunting DMs.

If one of those twenty replies SETUP and you do a $147 configuration, the door just paid for the month. That reply only happens if the PDF was useful and note 7 was a human.

What you never charge for here

Do not sell this suite as a $9 lead magnet. That is passing this book off as yours, and it is also the wrong price for a book you do not own. This suite is The Operator Suite. It is not inventory. Do not charge for the sequence. Do not charge to unsubscribe. Do not charge to hear their score.

Refunds

The door is free, so there is nothing to refund on the magnet. For the playbook the sequence sells, refund on request in the first 7 or 14 days with no speech. Put that sentence on the checkout. A fight over $29 costs more than $29.

If they bought thinking the free action would be done for them, refund and fix the listing. If they only wanted the PDF, they already have it. That was always free.

When to raise the paid next step

Raise the playbook from $19 to $29 when ten strangers have bought it through the door. Raise to $47 when the file has templates and a 14-day plan. Do not raise the door. The door stays free.

Raise because the paid file does more, not because you got bored of $29. Email the extra page free to people who already paid. The sequence's sticky note changes the price. It does not add a second product.

A $97-$197 live hour of their results is allowed after they have the PDF, sold as itself. Mention it once in note 7 as SETUP only if you actually offer it. A fake SETUP is how you spend Thursday on discovery calls you did not price.

The first 72 hours

Day 1 morning: the sticky note

Write the paid next step on a sticky note. Title and price. That is the only thing the sequence is allowed to sell. If you cannot name it, stop. Finish the product. A door into an empty house is a hobby, and hobbies do not get sequences.

Day 1 late morning: seven questions that change the advice

Write seven questions that change the advice. Not flattery. Each answer should send them toward a different next step: a playbook, a skill pack, do not buy anything yet — finish one job, or talk to a person, not a file.

Draft them as multiple choice. Free text is how you get novels and never score them. If two answers never change the PDF, delete one question and merge them. Read them out loud. If you would not answer them on a phone in a van, they are too cute.

How you know a question changes the advice: write the free action for answer A and for answer B. If those two sentences are the same, the question is a decoration. Are you an ambitious entrepreneur does not change anything. Do you have one offer a stranger can buy this week without a call does. Yes points at a pack. Not yet points at write the offer sentence this week, do not buy a course.

Sit with a person who does the job, or with your own last month of notes. Ask what actually changes the next step. Hours available. Saved project or blank chat. One offer or not. Where customers find them. Those change the band. Motivational mood does not.

Day 1 afternoon: the scoring key and three bands

Zero to two points per question. Three bands, not twelve. Example: 0-5 still-setup, 6-10 ready-for-a-pack, 11-14 ready-but-inconsistent. Write one sentence per band that a skeptical friend would accept. Fake precision (you are 73.4 percent AI-ready) is a toy. A fake 94 out of 100 is a flyer. Three bands is a diagnosis.

Put the key on page one of the PDF so they can audit you. Test the key with two fake answer sheets before you export. Sheet one should land in still-setup. Sheet two should land in ready-for-a-pack. If both land in the same band, three of your questions do not diagnose. Fix them this afternoon, not after ten strangers all score 8.

Day 1 night: the two-to-four page PDF

Two to four pages. How scoring works. What each band means. One action per band that does not require paying you. Your name. The year. A sentence that the file is free even if they never buy. Your email in the footer as a human, not as a funnel.

Page one: title, your name, the year, how the 0-2 scoring works, the three band ranges. Page two: what each band means, and the free action for each. Page three: one worked example of a free action, with the actual words they can reuse. Page four, if you need it: a small template, the deal in one line, your email.

Do not paste chapters of this suite. Do not put a fake 94/100 at the top. Export from Google Docs. Print it or open it on your phone. If type hits the edge, fix the margins tonight.

Quiet-page test before you sleep: delete every mention of the paid file. If the PDF still stands, you passed. If it collapses, you wrote a brochure. Rewrite the free actions until they stand alone.

Day 2: form live

MailerLite, Beehiiv, or Tally into either. Fields: first name optional, email required, the seven questions. Thank-you page includes the PDF now. If the form tool wants company size, budget, phone, mailing address — decline. Seven questions plus email. That is the whole form.

Put a one-sentence privacy line under the button: you are joining a short sequence, you can leave in one click. Put the form above the paid button on your page. The door is the first thing a stranger sees. The playbook is the second.

From-name is your first name, one word. Not MAIL-DAEMON. Not your LLC in all caps. A person they will recognize when note 2 arrives.

Day 2 night: the stranger test

Test as a stranger from a second email. Confirm the file arrives in under two minutes. Confirm the PDF opens on a phone. Confirm unsubscribe is one click and actually leaves. Confirm the thank-you page does not bury the file under a button labeled resources.

If delivery takes five minutes, that is a bug. Fix from-address, fix the automation, run the test again. Two passing runs. Then sleep.

Day 3 morning: the 5-7 note sequence

Write 5-7 notes before anyone joins. You will not write them later. You will panic and paste a pitch. Draft them in the tool.

  • Note 1: here is your file, read the band, do the action. Unsubscribe reminder.
  • Notes 2-4: teach. One job, one example, one mistake. No paid link unless they ask.
  • Notes 5-6: the playbook exists, price, link. A customer sentence if you have one.
  • Note 7: last time the link will be in the sequence, plus a quiet SETUP reply option if a human setup is truly the better fit. Unsubscribe reminder again.

Spacing: note 1 instant. Note 2 the next morning. Notes 3-4 every other day. Notes 5-7 with a day of air between them. Then silence until you have something useful. Daily blasts train them to skim, then to leave.

Day 3 afternoon: share once

Share it once in a place you already help people. One post, one comment, one email to people who already know you. Do not buy ads. Do not spray five platforms. Watch whether anyone finishes the seven questions. If they abandon at question two, the questions are too cute or too many.

Reply to the first stranger like a person. One sentence. Not a six-link kit. The 72 hours end when a human who is not you has the file.

The path, step by step

Step 1. Name the paid thing the door will sell

Usually path 1. Write the title and the price on a sticky note so the sequence does not wander into a buffet. If you cannot name it, stop. Finish the product. One paid thing. One price.

Step 2. Write seven questions that diagnose, not flatter

Sit with a person who does the job and ask what actually changes the next step. If two answers never change the PDF, delete one question and merge them. Multiple choice only. Seven is enough to change advice and short enough to finish on a phone. Read them out loud. If you would not answer them in a van, they are too cute.

Step 3. Write a scoring key with three bands you could defend

Zero to two points per question. Three bands, not fake precision. Example: 0-5 still-setup, 6-10 ready-for-a-pack, 11-14 ready-but-inconsistent. One sentence per band a skeptical friend would accept. Put the key on page one of the PDF so they can audit you. Run two fake answer sheets. If both land in the same band, rewrite three questions.

Step 4. Write the PDF so the free next step is real

Two to four pages. How scoring works. What each band means. One action per band that does not require paying you. Example: Run one recurring job in a saved project this week. Do not buy a second subscription. If the free action is buy my file, you failed the fairness test. Keep rewriting until a friend can act without a card. Print it. Open it on a phone. Fix the margins.

Step 5. Brand the scorecard as yours

Title, your name, the job, the year. This suite is The Operator Suite. You may brand your own scorecard. You may not copy this book, sell it as yours, or give it away as if you wrote it. A two-to-four page diagnostic you wrote is the product. This suite is not.

Step 6. Build the form and hook it to a real list tool

Email required. Instant file. No 40 fields. No company size, budget, phone, mailing address. First name is optional. Seven questions. A one-sentence privacy line under the button: you are joining a short sequence, you can leave in one click. MailerLite, Beehiiv, or Tally into either. Tag the score band if you can do it without a science project. If you cannot, send one sequence to everyone and mention bands in the PDF only. Do not delay launch for a tagging architecture.

Step 7. Write 5-7 notes before anyone joins

Teach, then ask. Note 1 is the file, the band, the action, and an unsubscribe reminder. Notes 2-4 teach: one job, one example, one mistake, no paid link. Notes 5-6 ask for the playbook: price, link, a customer sentence if you have one. Note 7 is a quiet close or a single SETUP mention if a human is truly the better fit, plus unsubscribe again. Draft them in the tool. You will not write them later.

Step 8. Test delivery and the path 1 checkout from a second email

Fill the form as a stranger. File in under two minutes, on the thank-you screen and in note 1. PDF opens on a phone. Unsubscribe is one click and actually leaves. Then test-buy the paid checkout from that same second email. Click every link in the sequence as if you were tired and suspicious. The sequence must not point at a dead button. Fix the from-name so it looks like a person.

Step 9. Put the form above the paid button and share once

A stranger who hits the page should see the diagnostic first. Share once where you already help. One post. One room. Not five platforms before you know delivery works. Do not buy ads. Watch whether anyone finishes question two. If they drop, the questions are the bug, not the room.

Step 10. Reply to the first stranger like a person

One sentence that proves you read their score or their reply. Not a six-link kit. Not an auto-responder that says circle back. This is how a list starts feeling like a room. If they scored 8, say so, and point at the free action in their band. Then stop typing.

Step 11. After ten subscribers, read where they drop

Question two? The questions are cute. Thank-you page? Delivery is buried. Note 5? You asked too early or you were boring. Fix the drop. Do not buy a new tool. Do not add a webinar because the PDF felt thin. The PDF is thin on purpose. Teach in the notes.

Step 12. Ads only after the sequence exists — and keep a one-line sheet

Only then consider a small ad budget. Sequence first. Ads on an empty sequence buy you unsubscribes you paid for. Send ads to the form, never to the paid button, until the form-to-email rate is something you can live with. Keep a one-line spreadsheet: date, source, score band, opened note 1, clicked playbook, bought, replied. Thirty rows is enough to see the truth. A dashboard before thirty people is costume jewelry.

A worked example: Noor's 7-question door

Noor finished a $29 playbook: a 10-day content system for solo trades. Friends bought it. Strangers did not know Noor existed. Noor needed a door, not a second book. Noor is the operator building a door. Noor did not write this suite. The scorecard is hers. The Operator Suite is not.

The situation

The playbook worked for people who already trusted Noor. The checkout was live. A second Gmail had already test-bought it. What was missing was a stranger. Noor had helped in a Facebook group for solo trades for a year — answers, not pitches. That room was the share, later. First: seven questions, three bands, a four-page PDF, a sequence written before anyone joined. Sticky note: 10-day content system for solo trades, $29.

The seven questions, and why each one

Each is multiple choice. Each changes the band. Noor sat with last month's DMs and asked what actually changed the advice she gave.

  1. In the last 30 days, how many times did you actually finish a job with AI, not just open a chat? (0, 1-3, 4+). Zero is still-setup. This stops the person who thinks opening a chat counts as a system.
  2. Do you have one offer a stranger can buy this week without a call? (yes / not yet). Not yet: write the offer sentence, do not buy a course. Yes: a pack can help.
  3. Where does a new customer usually find you? (word of mouth, Google, Instagram or TikTok, they don't). They don't is a different next step than Google.
  4. What happens after someone messages you? (you reply yourself, a form, nothing for days). Nothing for days is operations. A content pack will not fix a silent inbox.
  5. Have you saved a prompt or a project you reuse, or do you start from a blank chat every time? (saved / blank). Blank is expensive. Middle-band free action: save one project and run it on a real job by Friday.
  6. How many hours a week can you give this, honestly, with the job you already have? (under 2, 2-5, 6+). Under 2 means pick one platform, not five.
  7. If a file told you the next step, would you rather have a pack to run yourself, or a person to set it up? (pack / person). This is how note 7 knows whether SETUP is honest. Some people should not buy a file.

Scoring and the three bands

Noor scores 0-2 points per question. Bands: 0-5 still-setup, 6-10 ready-for-a-pack, 11-14 ready-but-inconsistent. The PDF gives one action per band. Still-setup: write the offer sentence this week, do not buy a course. Ready-for-a-pack: run one saved project on a real job by Friday. Ready-but-inconsistent: pick one platform for 14 days. None of those actions require $29. That is the deal Noor keeps. Three bands, not a fake 94.

The four-page PDF

Page one: Trades AI scorecard — Noor, the year, how 0-2 scoring works, the three ranges. Page two: the three band meanings and the free action for each. Page three: a worked example of the saved-project action, with the actual prompt Noor uses on one finished job, names blurred. Page four: the deal in one line (free even if you never buy), Noor's email as a human, no pitch above the fold.

Quiet-page test: Noor deleted the one line that mentioned the $29 file. The PDF still stood. A friend who runs a lawn crew took the still-setup action without paying.

The form and the sequence

Email required. PDF on the thank-you page and in note 1. Noor brands it Trades AI scorecard — Noor — a scorecard, not this book. Tally into MailerLite. First name optional. Seven questions. Privacy line under the button. From-name: Noor.

Notes, drafted in the tool on Thursday morning before the share: (1) here is your file, read the band, do the action, unsubscribe is at the bottom; (2) a one-job example from the playbook, no pitch; (3) why blank chat is expensive, still no pitch; (4) a mistake: posting on five platforms; (5) the playbook exists, $29, link; (6) a customer sentence from a friend who used day 3; (7) last time the link will be in the sequence, plus a SETUP reply option, plus unsubscribe again.

The week it ran

Monday night: questions and scoring key. Two fake answer sheets. One landed at 3, one at 9. Good. Tuesday night: PDF, four pages, printed on the kitchen table, margins fixed. Wednesday: Tally into MailerLite, test from a second Gmail, file arrived in 40 seconds. Unsubscribe worked. Thursday morning: sequence drafted in the tool. Thursday 11am: one post in a Facebook group for solo trades Noor had helped in for a year, no pitch except the form.

A stranger named Dell finishes the form on Thursday 4:12pm. Score 8, ready-for-a-pack. Note 1 goes out at once. Noor writes Dell one sentence: Score 8 — do the saved project on one real job before you open another tab. Dell does the saved-project action on Friday and replies already did. Note 5 sells Saturday morning. Dell buys the $29 file Saturday 9:41am. Noor never ran an ad.

What almost broke it

Question 3 originally had six options including a joke. Two people dropped there in the first hour. Noor cut it to four options. Delivery originally linked the PDF under a button labeled resources. Dell's cousin (test inbox) missed it. Noor put the file above the fold on the thank-you page and in the first sentence of note 1. A fairness-test friend said page three was starting to feel like a brochure. Noor cut it back to one worked example.

Ninety days later

First email from someone Noor had never met: Thursday 4:12pm. That is the first sale of this path — the address, not the $29. The $29 is path 1 working through the door. Count both.

64 emails from strangers. 7 playbook sales through the sequence. 1 SETUP reply that became a $147 evening. Unsubscribe rate 3 percent. Score-band mix: some still-setup, most ready-for-a-pack, a few ready-but-inconsistent. Noor still has not run an ad. The door is a form, a file, and notes that teach. That is the whole machine.

Copy you can actually send

Swap the job. Keep the constraints. Do not add hype. Fill the brackets. Send.

The public line

Seven questions. A score. One next step. Free even if you never buy.

The post

I made a short AI-readiness scorecard for [your people]. Seven questions, a score, one thing to do this week. It is useful if you never buy from me. Link: [form].

The shorter post and the DM

Shorter post: Seven questions for [job]. You get a score and one next step. Email required. File is instant. You can leave any time.

DM to someone who already knows you: I built a 7-question scorecard for [job]. Thought of you because of [specific thing they said]. It is free. If it is not useful, ignore me. [form]

Sales page hero

Find out where you actually are with AI for [job]. Seven questions. A score. One next step you can do this week even if you never buy. Start here: [form]

Put that above the paid button. The playbook listing can sit below. A stranger should hit the diagnostic first.

Checkout blurb for the playbook the door sells

This is the 10-day file the scorecard points at. If the free action was enough, you do not need this. If you want the full sequence, it is $29. Refund if you ask in 14 days.

Note 1 (instant)

Your scorecard is here: [PDF]. Read the band with your score. Do the one action this week. I will send a few short notes. You can leave any time — unsubscribe is at the bottom.

That is the whole note. Do not add a bio. Do not add a second PDF. Do not add the paid link.

Notes 2-4, teach

Note 2: One job. Here is how I run [specific task] without a blank chat. No link to anything paid. If you already did this week's action, reply with the word DONE and I will leave you alone until the next note.

Note 3: Why a blank chat is expensive for [job]. One mistake I made. One constraint you can paste. Still no pitch.

Note 4: A mistake: posting on five platforms, buying a second subscription, writing 40 questions. Pick one. The free action in your PDF is still the assignment.

Notes 5-7, the ask

Note 5: If you want the full sequence I use for [job], it is a $29 playbook: [link]. If the free action in the PDF is enough, stay with that. Either is fine.

Note 6: A sentence from someone who used day 3. Then the same link. Then a reminder they can leave.

Note 7: Last note in this set. Playbook is still here: [link]. If you want a human setup instead, reply with the word SETUP and I will tell you the price. If not, I will write when I have something useful. Unsubscribe anytime.

If you do not offer a human setup, delete the SETUP sentence. Do not invent a service in note 7.

Refund reply, and what you do not write

Refund (for the playbook, not the door): Done. Refunded. Keep the file if you already downloaded it. If the scorecard was the useful part, that was always free.

Do not paste chapters of this suite into your PDF. Do not put a fake 94/100 at the top. Do not forget the unsubscribe. Your scorecard is yours. This book is not. The public line is seven questions, a score, one next step, free even if you never buy.

Week-by-week if you have a job

Assume evenings. This is four weeks to a working door, not a content brand. No ads in week 1. No webinar in week 2. No second magnet in week 3.

Week 1

  • Day 1: sticky note, seven questions, scoring key, two fake answer sheets, PDF draft.
  • Day 2: PDF export, fairness test with a friend, form live, test as a stranger, fix delivery.
  • Day 3: 5-7 notes in the tool, share once where you already help.
  • Day 4: reply to humans. Do not add a webinar. Do not open a second platform.
  • Day 5: read drop-off. Cut a cute question. Move the PDF above the fold if people miss it.
  • Day 6: one more share in the same room, or a personal email to five people who already trust you. Not ads.
  • Day 7: count emails from strangers, not likes. If zero, the share was in the wrong room or the first line of the post was a pitch.

Week 2

Reply to humans. Fix the question people skip. Do not add a webinar. Count emails from strangers, not likes on the post. Rewrite note 1 if the click rate on the PDF is embarrassing. Rewrite note 5 if nobody clicks the playbook and you asked in note 2 by accident.

If you have a job, this week is 30-40 minutes a night: ten minutes of replies, twenty minutes of one fix, ten minutes of not touching it.

Week 3

If ten people finished the form and the sequence is live, you may share again or spend a small amount on ads to the form — not to the paid button. If fewer than ten, the share was weak or the questions feel like a trap. Tighten the PDF's free action. Do not buy traffic to a flyer.

Tag score bands if you still have not, only if it is easy. Otherwise leave it. Teaching one sequence to everyone is allowed.

Week 4

Read the spreadsheet. Form starts versus finishes. Unsubscribes. Playbook clicks. Replies. One genuine reply is worth twenty silent opens.

Decide one change, not five. Either a question, or the PDF action, or the note 5 sentence. Ship the change. Do not rebuild the brand.

If the door produced emails and no cash, that is still this path working. Path 1 cash may land in month two. Keep the sequence. Do not panic-add a webinar.

After week 4

A monthly share in the room you already help. A monthly PDF tweak if a question is dated. That is maintenance, not a new product. The door is not a content calendar. Do not write a second scorecard for a second job until thirty strangers have finished the first. Later products get later notes, after this sequence ends.

If zero strangers wrote back

The failure is usually the room, the first line, or question two. Not the market. Not the logo. Share in the place you already help, with a first line that is the seven questions, not your bio. Cut a cute option. Run the stranger test again. Send five personal emails to people who already trust you. Then wait a week. Do not buy ads to diagnose a flyer. Fix the flyer first.

The quality bar

The bar is a file that still helps if they never pay, and a score that would change if they answered honestly.

Voice

Kitchen table, not conference stage. Short sentences. Named job. Named next step. If a paragraph could run in a motivational clip, cut it. Read page one out loud. If you would not say it, it does not ship.

Questions

They change the advice. Are you an ambitious entrepreneur does not. Do you have one offer a stranger can buy this week does.

Below-bar: five questions that all output you should buy my course. Above-bar: seven questions a practitioner would recognize as their Tuesday. Multiple choice. Four options or fewer. No jokes in the options. No free text on v1.

PDF

Two to four pages. Band meanings. One free action each. Your name. The year. No pasted chapters from someone else's book. You may brand your own scorecard. You may not copy this book and sell it as yours.

Below-bar: 14 pages, your origin story, a fake 94, a pitch on every page. Above-bar: they can do the action tonight with the PDF and nothing else. Margins that survive a phone. Filename a human can find.

Sequence

Teaches first. Asks later. Unsubscribe always. Instant file, always. 5-7 notes, written before anyone joins.

Below-bar: note 1 is a 1,200-word pitch. Above-bar: note 1 is the file, the band, the action, a way out. Notes 2-4 have no paid link. Notes 5-7 have one paid thing, the one on the sticky note.

Ethics you do not get to skip

This suite is The Operator Suite. Passing this book off as yours is off limits. Selling this book as your own is off limits. Giving this book away as a magnet with your logo on the cover is off limits. Building a door that points at your playbook is the work.

You may quote a sentence of this path in your own words. You may not export the suite. If you are unsure, you already know.

Five tests you can run this week

  1. Friend fairness test: they can act without paying. Two friends if you can — one who does the job, one who does not.
  2. Stranger delivery test: second inbox, file in under two minutes, PDF opens on a phone.
  3. Unsubscribe test: one click, actually leaves.
  4. Scoring test: two different answer sheets produce two different bands and two different actions.
  5. Quiet-page test: delete every mention of the paid file from the PDF. If the PDF still stands, you passed. If it collapses, you wrote a brochure.

Fail any one of those and you are not sharing yet. These are not vibes. These are pass or rewrite.

Below the bar

A fake 94 out of 100. A 40-field form. A 14-page sales letter. This suite with your name on the cover. Note 1 as a pitch. No unsubscribe. Delivery tomorrow. Ads on day one. Questions that always output the same band. If a tired stranger cannot finish seven questions and do one free action this week, it is below the bar.

What to count

First week

  • Form starts versus finishes. If half leave, you have too many questions or they smell a quiz trap.
  • Emails from people you have never met. That is the first sale of this path.
  • Whether the PDF link is clicked. If not, delivery is buried.
  • Time from submit to file in the test inbox. Over five minutes is a bug.
  • Unsubscribe works, yes or no. If no, you are not counting anything else yet.

After 30 subscribers

  • Unsubscribe rate. Over 5 percent on the sequence means you asked too early or you were boring. Under 1 percent and zero clicks can mean nobody is reading — check the from-name.
  • Playbook click from notes 5-7. A few percent is real. Fifty percent means you only invited fans.
  • Replies. One genuine reply is worth twenty silent opens.
  • Score-band mix. If everyone lands in the same band, the questions do not diagnose.

Thirty is enough to see a pattern. Ten is enough to see a drop. Do not wait for a hundred to fix question two.

Day 90

  • Stranger emails total.
  • Playbook sales that can be traced to the sequence.
  • SETUP replies, if you offer a human.
  • Cost of ads, if any, versus emails. If you paid $80 for 4 emails, the post in the room you already help was cheaper. Stop the ads. Fix the door.
  • Unsubscribe rate across the whole sequence, not one note.

What to ignore

Likes on the post. Follower count. Time on page. Heatmaps. Open-rate vanity if your tool lies. A brand awareness story. Ignore anything that is not an email, a reply, or a checkout. A door with 12 form finishes and 3 genuine replies is healthier than a post with 400 reactions and zero emails.

The one-line spreadsheet

date | source | score band | note1 clicked | playbook clicked | bought | replied

That is the whole dashboard. Thirty rows. A notebook is allowed. Fill it the day they join, not in a monthly panic. If the source column is always ads and unsub is ugly, stop the ads.

Ads math

Ads are allowed after the sequence exists, delivery works, and a handful of strangers have finished the form. Send them to the form. Cost per email is the number. If a weekend in the room you already help produced more emails than $80 of ads, the ads are the sick part. Kill them. Fix the door. Do not raise budget on a flyer.

Objections you will hear — including your own

People will not give an email

Some will not. They were not going to buy this month. The people who want the score will. Do not open the PDF to the whole internet and then wonder why you have no list. Email required is the deal. Unsubscribe is the other half of the deal. Both.

A free file should be a 40-page guide

No. Long and useless is still useless. Seven questions and a tight PDF beat a stolen book with your logo.

Can I just upload this suite as the magnet

No. This suite is The Operator Suite. You may not copy this book, sell it as yours, or give it away as if you wrote it. Write a scorecard for your people. Point at your playbook. A stolen encyclopedia is theft and it is also a magnet nobody finishes.

I should run ads on day one

Not before the sequence exists. Paid traffic into silence is how you learn to hate lists. Ads after delivery works, a handful of strangers have finished, and the notes are live. Ads to the form, never to the paid button, until you can live with the form-to-email rate.

Fake scores convert better

They convert once. Then they tell friends. Your name is small. Keep it clean. Three bands you can defend will still be on your computer in a year. A fake 94 will be a screenshot in a group chat.

What if they only want the free thing

Good. You kept the deal. Some of them buy in three months. Some never do. That is allowed. A list of people who used a free action is worth more than a list of people who feel tricked.

I do not have a list to share with

You have a room you already help, or you do not have a door yet. One group, one comment thread, five personal emails. That is a share. A cold ad account is not a share. If you have never helped in a room, go help for a month. Then the form.

Beehiiv is too much

Then MailerLite. Then Tally into either. The tool is not the path. If you stall on tools, you are avoiding the questions. Write the questions on paper first. Pick a tool on Day 2, not on Day 1 at noon.

I will write the notes when people join

You will not. You will panic and paste a pitch. Write the notes on Day 3, before the share. 5-7. Teach, then ask.

GDPR, privacy, my cousin in the EU

Say what they are joining, in one sentence, under the button. Include unsubscribe. Do not buy lists. Do not scrape emails out of comments. That is the whole compliance program for a seven-question scorecard.

What this feeds — and what feeds it

The door is last for a reason. It feeds every other path and it needs one of them first. Friends and DMs are how the first playbooks sell. The door is how strangers join that line. If you build the door first, you have a porch on an empty house.

What must exist

A paid next step, almost always path 1. Optionally a service or a setup if the diagnostic band says person, not file. The sequence should not invent a product you have not shipped.

A skill pack (path 2), a prompt stack (path 3), or a productized service (path 7) can be the paid next step if that is what you actually sell. Pick one. Write it on the sticky note. Test-buy it from a second email before the form goes live.

What the list then feeds

  • Playbook sales without you DMing.
  • Later drops (path 17): you can tell a list about a Thursday live without begging the algorithm.
  • Research briefs, automations, custom projects — only as a reply offer, not as note 1.
  • A newsletter if you want one. The door can be the same form. The letter is a Tuesday. The door is how they arrived.
  • A quiet operator group (path 15): you invite people who already shipped, not lurkers who wanted a free PDF.

The list is the asset. Everything else is a later sentence to people who already have a reason to open you.

What the door must never feed

A replica of this suite with your name on it. A free file that is only a sales letter. A purchased list. Those rot. This suite is The Operator Suite. It is not a magnet, not a white-label, not inventory. Your scorecard is the magnet. Your playbook is the house.

Upstream

If you have no playbook, this path is closed. If you have no checkout, this path is closed. If you have never sold to a person who knows you, sell to them first. The door is for strangers. Strangers are later.

Pick one paid next step

The sticky note holds one title and one price. If you have a playbook and a skill pack, the door points at one. The other can wait for a later note, after this sequence ends. One next step. Named. Priced. Live.

Mistakes that kill the door

Buying ads before the sequence exists. A 40-field form. Fake scores. Forgetting the unsubscribe. Those still kill it. The rest, with recovery this week:

1. A PDF that is only a sales letter

Recovery: run the quiet-page test tonight. Delete every paid mention. Rewrite until the free action stands alone. Two to four pages. One action per band. Fairness-test a friend tomorrow.

2. Passing this book off as yours

Selling this book as your own, or giving it away as a magnet with your logo, kills the door and your name. This suite is The Operator Suite. Recovery: delete that file today. Write seven questions for your job. You will be late. You will also still have a name.

3. We will send the file in 24 hours

A drip trick. They already answered. Recovery: put the PDF on the thank-you page tonight, and in the first sentence of note 1. Instant means under two minutes, not someday.

4. Asking for the sale in paragraph one of the free file

Recovery: move the ask to notes 5-7. The PDF keeps the band and the free action. The sticky note keeps the paid thing in the sequence, not on page one.

5. Daily blasts

Recovery: 5-7 notes, then silence until you have something useful. Note 1 instant. Then air. Daily is how you become noise, then a statistic in the unsub column.

6. Questions that always output the same band

Recovery: two fake answer sheets this afternoon. If the band does not change, rewrite three questions. Flattery is not a diagnostic. Do you want to grow is not a question.

7. Sharing on five platforms before you tested delivery

Recovery: one room. Test inbox first. Second Gmail, phone, timer. Two passing runs. Then one share. Platforms two through five wait until strangers finish the form.

8. From-name that looks like a robot

Recovery: your first name, one word. Not MAIL-DAEMON. Not the LLC. A person they will open tomorrow.

9. Tagging architecture that delays launch

Recovery: one sequence for everyone. Mention bands in the PDF. Launch. Tag later if it is easy. Thirty strangers do not need HubSpot.

10. A webinar bolted on because the PDF felt thin

Recovery: the PDF is thin on purpose. Teach in the notes, not on Zoom. Two to four pages, 5-7 notes. If the free action is real, thin is a feature.

If you catch yourself rewriting the PDF to mention the paid file more than the free action, you slipped. Put the paid file back in notes 5-7.

Tools — only what you need

A form, a PDF scorecard, MailerLite or Beehiiv. That is the stack.

The stack

Nothing else is required for v1. Google Docs to write. A form to ask. A list tool to send 5-7 notes and to honor unsubscribe. A checkout you already have from an earlier path. A second email to test. A phone to open the PDF.

Form

Tally, the Beehiiv form, or MailerLite's. Email required. Seven questions. Thank-you with the file. Tally is the $0 path if you already have a place to host the PDF. Decline company size, budget, phone, mailing address. First name optional. Privacy line under the button.

PDF

Google Docs export. Two to four pages. Your name, the year, a sentence that the file is free even if they never buy. Print one page. If the margins fail, fix them before you share. Open it on a phone. Filename: job-scorecard-yourname.pdf. No Canva rabbit hole. A cover that states the job is enough.

Sequence

5-7 notes in the same tool. Plain text is fine. No twenty-pixel buttons in every paragraph. From-name is your name. Note 1 is automated on submit. The rest are a simple delay. You do not need a journey builder with twelve branches.

Checkout for the paid next step

Stripe Payment Link or Stan. Test-buy from a second email. The door does not replace this. The door points at it in notes 5-7. If the checkout is not live, the door is closed.

Do not add yet

Do not add a webinar platform, a quiz app with 14 branches, or a CRM. Thirty strangers do not need HubSpot. They need a file and a way out. Do not add a popup that fights the form.

The $0 path

Google Docs. Tally free. A MailerLite free tier or Beehiiv free tier. Stripe Payment Link for the playbook. That is enough to get the first stranger email. Buy tools after thirty people, not before.

Setup order

Sticky note. Seven questions on paper. Scoring key. PDF in Docs. Fairness test. Export. Form. Connect the list tool. Note 1 delivers the file. Notes 2-7 drafted. Stranger test from a second inbox. Unsubscribe test. Checkout test. Then share once. Do not compare six form builders on Day 1. Write the questions first.

Checklist

Before you write a question

  • You finished an earlier path; the paid next step exists
  • The paid next step has a live checkout you have test-bought
  • Sticky note with the one paid thing the sequence may sell, title and price
  • You can name the free action in one sentence
  • You are writing your own scorecard, not exporting this suite

Before the form goes live

  • Seven questions that change the advice
  • Scoring key you can defend to a skeptical friend
  • Three bands, not fake precision, not a fake 94
  • Two fake answer sheets land in two different bands
  • PDF with one free action per band
  • PDF still works if every paid mention is deleted
  • You did not copy this book into the PDF
  • You did not put your name on this book and call it a magnet
  • Your name, the year, and free even if you never buy on the PDF
  • Filename a human can find; PDF opens on a phone

Before you share

  • Email required, not 40 fields
  • First name optional
  • Privacy line under the button, one sentence
  • Instant delivery, tested from a second inbox, under two minutes
  • File is on the thank-you page and in note 1
  • Unsubscribe works, tested, one click
  • 5-7 notes written before you share widely
  • Teach first, ask later (notes 5-7)
  • From-name is a human
  • Form sits above the paid button

After the first stranger

  • Shared once where you already help
  • No ads until the sequence exists
  • First stranger email treated like a person, one sentence
  • Spreadsheet: date, source, band, clicks, bought, replied
  • Drop-off read after ten finishes; one fix, not five
  • Ads, if any, point at the form, not the paid button

The rule, in one block

  • This suite is The Operator Suite
  • You may brand your own scorecard
  • You may not copy this book, sell it as yours, or give it away as if you wrote it
  • The public name is a scorecard for a job, with your name, not the name of this book

FAQ

Do I have to use seven questions?

Seven is enough to change advice and short enough to finish on a phone. Five can work. Forty cannot. Default: seven, multiple choice.

What if I do not have a playbook yet?

Do not build the door. Finish path 1, or another path with a named next step. An empty house does not need a nicer porch.

Can I brand the scorecard with my business name?

Yes. You may brand your own scorecard. You may not copy this book, sell it as yours, or give it away as if you wrote it. The public name is [Job] scorecard — [you]. This suite is The Operator Suite. Those are different objects.

Can I give this suite away as my lead magnet?

No. This suite is The Operator Suite. You may not copy this book, sell it as yours, or give it away as if you wrote it. A two-to-four page diagnostic you wrote for one job is the door. This book is not a magnet. If you already exported it with your logo, delete that file today and write seven questions.

MailerLite or Beehiiv?

Whichever you will actually open. Beehiiv if you also want a public letter. MailerLite if you want simple forms. Both handle unsubscribe. Use that feature. Default if you stall: Beehiiv, one form, one sequence.

Should the PDF include my prices?

A line at the end is allowed: If you want the full 10-day file, it lives here. The body of the PDF should still work with that line deleted. That is the quiet-page test. If the PDF collapses without the price, you wrote a brochure.

How fast is instant?

On the thank-you screen and in the first email. Under two minutes in a test inbox. Not check your promotions tab in a few hours while we wait to look hungry.

What is the first sale on this path?

The first email from someone you have never met. Cash from the playbook is path 1 using the door. Count both. Do not pretend the list is failing because the $29 did not happen on day one.

Can I sell the diagnostic as a $9 product?

Then it is not this path. This path is a free door. If you want a paid score, that is a small file on another path, and you still need a free door later. Do not charge $9 and also call it free.

What about GDPR and consent?

Say what they are joining, in one sentence, under the button. Include unsubscribe. Do not buy lists. Do not scrape emails out of comments. That is the whole program for a seven-question scorecard.

When do I add ads?

After the sequence exists, delivery works, and a handful of strangers have finished the form. Until then you are paying to learn that your PDF is a flyer. Send ads to the form, never to the paid button. If $80 bought you four emails, the room you already help was cheaper. Stop. Fix the door.

Can I use a Typeform quiz with 14 branches?

You can. You should not, for v1. Seven questions, one sequence. Branches are how you never launch. Tag bands later if it is easy. Do not delay the stranger test for a branching tree.

How long should the PDF be?

Two to four pages. If you need eight, you are writing a playbook. Sell that. Do not give a playbook away as a scorecard and then wonder why nobody buys the playbook.

Can I send the sequence from Gmail?

Not if you want unsubscribe and a straight face. Use a real tool. The $0 tiers exist. From-name is still your first name. The tool is what makes leave in one click true.
